docs.title: Module responsibilities
docs.text: Module Responsibility cli.py Typer commands: init, validate, plan, run, resume, rerun, list, show, compare, export, import, report, baseline set/show, check, drift, judge calibrate, rag sweep, cache clear, serve, metrics, tasks, providers. Installs the SIGINT handler and maps errors to exit codes. api/ FastAPI app factory, in-process job queue, request/response schemas, Prometheus telemetry. config/ Pydantic experiment schema (models.py), YAML loading with ConfigError (loader.py), environment settings (settings.py, LLMBENCH_*), pricing table (pricing.py). plugins/registry.py Generic Registry[T] with lazy entry-point discovery (ADR 0006). datasets/ Sample schema, JSONL/YAML loading with duplicate-id checks, canonical content hashing, stratified sampling. prompts/template.py Jinja2 SandboxedEnvironment with StrictUndefined; templates may only use input, context, documents, tags, metadata, sample_id, so the reference answer can never leak into a prompt. Templates are content-hashed into the manifest. providers/ Provider protocol, request/result types and ErrorClass taxonomy (base.py); mock (ADR 0007); OpenAI / OpenAI-compatible and Gemini adapters (ADR 0008); factory and availability checks (registry.py). tasks/base.py Task types defining parsing, the pass criterion, the mock oracle and default metrics. runner/ prepare.py (validated, loaded experiment and lazy grid), executor.py (workers, retries, breaker, budget, checkpointing), cache.py, manifest.py (reproducibility record and run id), plan.py (pre-flight estimates) (ADR 0002, ADR 0003). metrics/ Metric base classes and registry (base.py), bundles (consistency, latency, cost, reliability, safety), the evaluation engine (engine.py) that always adds pass, reliability, latency and cost metrics. judges/ Rubrics, the LLM judge, the llm_judge_correctness metric and calibration (ADR 0005). rag/ Ingestion, chunking, BM25 / vector / hybrid retrieval, reranking, cited generation, RAG metrics and rag sweep. The sweep calls providers directly, without the runner's rate limiter, retries, cache or run store. stats/ Bootstrap intervals, paired tests, effect sizes, multiple-comparison corrections, power and Cohen's kappa (ADR 0004). tracking/ ORM models and migrations, RunStore, run comparison, regression gates, drift detection (rolling robust z-score and CUSUM), run bundles. reporting/ RunSummary assembly, rich tables, self-contained HTML with inline SVG charts, Markdown for pull requests, CSV / Parquet / JSON export, Pareto front over quality, cost and latency. observability.py structlog configuration, redaction, optional OpenTelemetry spans. domain.py, errors.py, text.py, embeddings.py Shared records (TrialRecord, MetricValue), exception hierarchy rooted at LLMBenchError, text normalisation, deterministic hash embedder.

docs.title: Key invariants
docs.text:
• Core code never imports provider SDKs. pyproject.toml bans openai and google.genai through ruff's flake8-tidy-imports.banned-api (rule TID251); only providers/openai_provider.py, providers/gemini_provider.py and the provider test files are exempt. The adapters import their SDK lazily and the registry imports the adapters inside the factories, so pip install llmbench without extras works with the mock provider.
  • Every test runs offline. pytest's default addopts deselects -m live; real-API contract tests live in tests/live/ and are skipped without keys. Adapter unit tests inject an httpx2.MockTransport client. Time-dependent runner logic uses FakeClock.
  • Reproducibility via manifests. runner/manifest.py stores, per run: LLMBench version, Python and platform, git SHA, the full config and its hash, dataset path, full and evaluated content hashes and the evaluated sample ids, prompt template hashes, model specs, seeds, the pricing file and its as_of date, and the grid size. rerun re-creates a run from it; resume refuses when the evaluated dataset hash or a prompt template hash changed; comparisons refuse different dataset hashes unless --allow-dataset-drift.
  • The trial is the unit of persistence. Each trial is committed as soon as it finishes; trial_key is unique per run.
  • No hardcoded models or prices. Model names live in experiment YAML and prices in a user-supplied pricing.yaml; an unpriced model has cost_usd = None, not zero.
  • Secrets come from the environment only (Settings, SecretStr), never from config files.

docs.title: Extension points
docs.text:
• Providers: register a factory (ModelSpec, Settings) -> Provider with PROVIDERS.decorator(name) or the llmbench.providers entry point; raise ProviderError with an ErrorClass so retries and the breaker apply.
  • Metrics: subclass TrialMetric or GroupMetric with @register_metric, or decorate a function with @trial_metric; or publish under llmbench.metrics.
  • Tasks: subclass Task and register an instance in TASKS or under llmbench.tasks.
  • Judge rubrics: YAML files (criteria, scale, anchors) referenced from judge.rubric.
  • Gates: gates.yaml per repository (CI_EVAL_GATE.md).
  • Storage: any SQLAlchemy URL through LLMBENCH_DB_URL or --db.
  • RAG: retrievers and rerankers follow the Retriever protocol in rag/retrieval.py; vector stores sit behind one interface in rag/stores.py (numpy by default, optional pgvector).

docs.title: API service
docs.text:
llmbench serve starts api/app.py::create_app under uvicorn (default bind 127.0.0.1:8000).

  • Endpoints: POST /runs (queue an experiment, 202 with a job id), GET /runs, GET /jobs, GET /runs/{ref} (job status, or stored run metadata by id, prefix, baseline name or latest), GET /runs/{ref}/results (full RunSummary), POST /compare, GET /health, GET /metrics.
  • Job queue (api/jobs.py): an asyncio.Queue consumed by LLMBENCH_API_WORKERS (default 2) worker tasks in the server's event loop, each calling Runner.run. Job status lives in process memory; run results live in the database. To run several instances, replace JobQueue with an external queue (for example Arq on Redis, Celery or Cloud Tasks): the worker body stays Runner(store, settings, evaluator=evaluate_run).run(config) and all durable state is already in the shared database, which should then be Postgres rather than a SQLite file. On shutdown, workers are cancelled; trials already written stay in the store and the run can be continued with llmbench resume; the job is reported as failed with the reason "cancelled at server shutdown (resumable)".
  • Authentication: every route except /health, /metrics and the OpenAPI pages requires an X-API-Key header equal to LLMBENCH_API_KEY, compared with secrets.compare_digest. serve refuses to start without the key unless --insecure-no-auth is passed.
  • Request ids: a middleware takes X-Request-ID from the request or generates one, binds it into structlog context vars, echoes it in the response header and includes it in error bodies (ErrorResponse).
  • Prometheus metrics: a private CollectorRegistry per app exposes llmbench_http_requests (method, route, status), llmbench_http_request_duration_seconds, llmbench_runs (by status), llmbench_provider_requests (model, cached), llmbench_provider_errors (model, error class) and llmbench_provider_latency_seconds. Provider counters are updated when a run finishes, from its stored trials.
  • Workspace sandboxing: submitted configs are parsed with the workspace (LLMBENCH_WORKSPACE, default .) as base directory, and validate_workspace_paths rejects absolute paths or paths resolving outside it for dataset, pricing, judge.rubric and every prompt template / system_template. Symlinks are resolved before the check.
  • Errors: RunNotFoundError maps to 404, other LLMBenchErrors to 400.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
• Logging (observability.py): structlog to stderr, console or JSON (LLMBENCH_LOG_FORMAT, --log-format), with ISO UTC timestamps and context variables merged in. Runner events include run_started, run_resumed, run_finished; the judge factory logs judge_unavailable and judge_is_candidate.
  • Redaction: a processor replaces fields whose names look like secrets (api_key, secret, token, password, authorization) and masks secret-shaped values inside strings (sk-..., AIza..., Bearer ...). With LLMBENCH_REDACT_PROMPTS=true, prompt and output fields are also replaced. Settings hold keys as SecretStr.
  • Tracing: with LLMBENCH_OTEL_ENABLED=true and the otel extra installed, span() opens OpenTelemetry spans llmbench.run (run id, grid size), llmbench.trial (trial key, cache misses only) and llmbench.provider_call (provider, attempt). LLMBench only obtains a tracer; configuring a TracerProvider and exporter is left to the host process. Without the extra a warning is logged and spans become no-ops.

docs.title: CI eval gate
docs.text: llmbench check compares a candidate run against a stored baseline and fails the CI job when a gated metric regresses by more than a tolerance and the regression is statistically significant. This page explains the gate, the baseline workflow built on run bundles, and how to wire it into GitHub Actions or GitLab CI. Statistical details are in METHODOLOGY.md and ADR 0004.

docs.title: How the gate decides
docs.text:
tracking/gates.py::check calls compare_runs restricted to the gated metrics, then evaluates every gate on every configuration pair. Configurations are (model_id, prompt_id) pairs; by default the gate compares configurations present in both runs, or the single configuration of each run when both have exactly one. --pair base_model/prompt=cand_model/prompt (repeatable) pairs them explicitly.

For each gate and pair, the comparison reduces both runs to per-sample means on their common samples, computes a paired-bootstrap CI for the delta, runs the paired test (sign-flip permutation by default, McNemar for single-trial binary metrics) and adjusts p-values across the gated metrics with the configured correction. A gate fails when:

  1. the metric moved in the bad direction by more than max_drop (absolute units of the metric), and, if max_relative_drop is set and the baseline value is non-zero, also by more than max_relative_drop relative to the baseline; and
  2. the adjusted p-value is below alpha and the delta CI excludes zero.

A gate also fails when the metric is missing from either run or fewer than two samples align ("insufficient aligned data"). A drop beyond tolerance that is not significant passes, with the reason recorded. The direction comes from the gate's direction or, if omitted, from the metric's registered higher_is_better.

docs.title: gates.yaml
docs.text:
Schema (GateConfig, Gate; unknown keys are rejected):

Key Type Default Meaning alpha float in (0, 1) 0.05 Significance level for every gate. correction holm, bh, none holm Multiple-comparison adjustment across gated metrics. allow_dataset_drift bool false Compare runs with different dataset hashes (on common sample ids). gates list, at least one required Gated metrics. gates[].metric string required Registered metric name, e.g. pass, f1, latency_ms. gates[].direction higher_is_better, lower_is_better from registry Override the metric's direction. gates[].max_drop float >= 0 0.0 Absolute tolerance in the metric's units. gates[].max_relative_drop float >= 0 unset Additional relative tolerance (both must be exceeded). gates[].alpha float in (0, 1) unset Per-gate significance level.

examples/gates.yaml (also scaffolded by llmbench init):

alpha: 0.05
correction: holm
gates:
  - {metric: pass, max_drop: 0.02}
  - {metric: f1, max_drop: 0.03}
  - {metric: latency_ms, direction: lower_is_better, max_drop: 100}

Without --gates, check uses a single gate: pass with max_drop: 0.02. Every run computes pass, the reliability metrics, latency_ms, ttft_ms, tokens_per_second, queue_wait_ms and cost_usd (metrics/engine.py::ALWAYS_COMPUTED); other gated metrics must be listed in the experiment's metrics.

docs.title: llmbench check
docs.text:
llmbench check --baseline main --candidate latest --gates gates.yaml --output gate.md

--baseline (default main) and --candidate (default latest) accept a baseline name, run id, unique id prefix or latest. The command prints a table and, with --output, writes Markdown: the gate results followed by the full comparison (estimates, delta CIs, tests, adjusted p-values, effect sizes, per-sample regressions, tag breakdown).

Exit code Meaning 0 Every gate passed. 1 At least one gate failed (regression, missing metric or insufficient data). 2 Configuration or lookup error: gates file not found, run or baseline not found, ambiguous run prefix, runs with no common configuration, dataset hash mismatch without --allow-dataset-drift.

A gates file that exists but fails schema validation, or is not valid YAML, is reported as a configuration error (exit code 2), so it can never be mistaken for a regression.

docs.title: Stored-baseline workflow
docs.text:
CI jobs start with an empty database, so the baseline travels with the repository as a run bundle (tracking/bundle.py, format llmbench-run/1): run metadata, manifest, every trial and every metric value. Paths in the manifest are stored relative to the project root (the working directory at export time) and resolved against --base-dir (default .) on import, so run both commands from the repository root.

# once, locally or in a trusted job: produce and commit the baseline
llmbench run evals/experiment.yaml --yes --no-cache
llmbench export latest --output baselines/main.json
git add baselines/main.json

# in every CI job
llmbench import baselines/main.json --as-baseline main
llmbench run evals/experiment.yaml --yes
llmbench check --baseline main --gates evals/gates.yaml --output gate.md

export defaults to the JSON bundle format (--format csv or parquet produce flat trial tables instead, which cannot be imported). import refuses a run id that already exists unless --replace. The gate reads the baseline's stored trials and metric values; it does not re-execute or re-score the baseline. The imported run keeps its original created_at, so the candidate run is latest after it executes.

docs.title: Refreshing the baseline
docs.text:
Refresh after an intentional change (new prompt, new model, updated dataset) has been reviewed:

  1. On the default branch, run the experiment with --no-cache so the baseline reflects the provider's current behaviour rather than cached responses.
  2. llmbench export latest --output baselines/main.json.
  3. Open a pull request with the new bundle; the diff shows changed outputs per trial. Reviewers can run llmbench compare between the old and new bundle (import both with distinct baseline names) to see exactly what moved.

A dataset change always requires a refresh, because the gate refuses to compare runs with different dataset hashes (below).

docs.title: Choosing max_drop: tolerance versus detectability
docs.text:
max_drop says how large a regression matters; significance says whether the benchmark can tell it from noise. Every comparison reports the minimum detectable effect (mde, two-sided paired test at power 0.8, from the observed per-sample differences) and warns below 30 paired samples. Run the experiment twice with no change (for example two runs with caching disabled) and inspect the MDE with llmbench compare <run1> <run2> --format md:

  • If max_drop is well below the MDE, regressions between the two values will often be non-significant and pass. The gate is then effectively set at roughly the MDE, not at max_drop. Either accept that, or lower the MDE with more samples (largest effect) or more trials per sample (reduces within-sample noise).
  • If max_drop is above the MDE, small but real changes are detected statistically but tolerated by design. This is usually the right setting for noisy metrics such as latency_ms.
  • stats.power.required_samples(sd_diff, effect) estimates how many samples are needed to detect a given effect.

docs.title: Why dataset changes fail the gate
docs.text: Each run stores the content hash of the samples actually evaluated (after sampling). Different samples have different difficulty, so a metric difference between two datasets cannot be attributed to the system under test. check therefore exits 2 on a hash mismatch. Passing --allow-dataset-drift (or allow_dataset_drift: true) compares on the intersection of sample ids and adds a note to the report; use it deliberately, for example when samples were only appended, and refresh the baseline afterwards.

docs.title: GitHub Actions example (another repository)
docs.text:
The repository under test commits evals/experiment.yaml, evals/gates.yaml, the dataset and prompts it references, and baselines/main.json. Pin LLMBench to a commit so the gate's statistics do not change underneath you.

name: LLM eval gate
on:
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  eval-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      LLMBENCH_DB_URL: sqlite:///${{ github.workspace }}/.llmbench/ci.db
      OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install LLMBench
        # or, for a vendored copy: pip install "./tools/llmbench[openai]"
        run: pip install "llmbench[openai] @ git+https://github.com/PiyushDas-2004/LLM-Bench@<commit-sha>"
      - name: Import stored baseline
        run: llmbench import baselines/main.json --as-baseline main
      - name: Run candidate experiment
        run: llmbench run evals/experiment.yaml --yes --strict-models
      - name: Eval gate
        run: llmbench check --baseline main --gates evals/gates.yaml --output gate.md
      - name: Publish gate report
        if: always()
        run: '[ -f gate.md ] && cat gate.md >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY" || true'

Notes:

  • llmbench run exits 2 if the cost estimate exceeds cost_confirm_threshold_usd without --yes, and 3 if the run ended budget_exceeded or partial; either stops the job before the gate, which is intended.
  • --strict-models turns a missing key or placeholder model name into an error instead of a silently skipped model.

docs.title: Real providers and secrets
docs.text:
• Store keys as repository or environment secrets (OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, or the variable named by a model's api_key_env). Keys are read only from the environment.
  • Pull requests from forks do not receive secrets; restrict the job to same-repository pull requests or run the mock-provider variant for forks.
  • Set budget.max_usd and budget.max_requests in the experiment; llmbench plan prints an upper-bound estimate (it needs a pricing.yaml entry for each model).
  • Pin dated model snapshots in the experiment YAML where the provider offers them; an alias that moves will register as a regression or improvement unrelated to your change.
  • Set rate_limit to your account limits. Limits apply per provider endpoint (provider, base_url, api_key_env), shared by all models that use it.

docs.title: GitLab CI
docs.text:
eval-gate:
  image: python:3.12-slim
  variables:
    LLMBENCH_DB_URL: "sqlite:///$CI_PROJECT_DIR/.llmbench/ci.db"
  script:
    - pip install "llmbench[openai] @ git+https://github.com/PiyushDas-2004/LLM-Bench@<commit-sha>"
    - llmbench import baselines/main.json --as-baseline main
    - llmbench run evals/experiment.yaml --yes --strict-models
    - llmbench check --baseline main --gates evals/gates.yaml --output gate.md
  artifacts:
    when: always
    paths: [gate.md]

python:3.12-slim has no git; install it first or use a full Python image. Define OPENAI_API_KEY as a masked CI/CD variable.

docs.title: Dogfooding: this repository's gate
docs.text:
.github/workflows/eval-gate.yml gates LLMBench with LLMBench, fully offline on the mock provider:

  1. imports baselines/gate-demo.json (a bundle of examples/gate/baseline.yaml) as main;
  2. runs examples/gate/noise.yaml, which changes only mock_seed (sampling noise), and requires llmbench check --baseline main --gates examples/gates.yaml to pass;
  3. runs examples/gate/regression.yaml, which lowers the mock accuracy from 0.85 to 0.40, and requires the same check to exit 1;
  4. appends both Markdown reports to the job summary.

Mock-provider numbers are illustrative and say nothing about any real model. The gate Markdown does not carry the mock banner that the HTML and run reports show, so label such summaries in the workflow when publishing them.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
This document states what LLMBench measures, how each number is computed, which assumptions those computations rest on, and where they break down. Every definition below is taken from the code; module paths are given so each claim can be checked. For the RAG-specific pipeline and metrics see RAG_EVALUATION.md.

Numbers in this document are either derived from a formula (the arithmetic is shown) or quoted from mock-provider runs, which are labelled as illustrative. No number here describes the quality of any real model.

docs.title: 1. Experiment model
docs.text:
An experiment (ExperimentConfig, src/llmbench/config/models.py) is a grid

\[ \text{grid} = \text{models} \times \text{prompts} \times \text{samples} \times \text{trials}, \qquad |\text{grid}| = M \cdot P \cdot N \cdot T . \]

Each cell is a WorkItem(model, prompt_id, sample, trial_index) with the key model_id|prompt_id|sample_id|trial_index (runner/prepare.py). A configuration is a (model_id, prompt_id) pair; every statistic is computed per configuration.

  • iter_items expands the grid trial-major (all samples for trial 0, then trial 1, ...), so a run stopped early by a budget or interrupt has covered every configuration and sample evenly rather than finishing some configurations and skipping others.
  • Optional subsampling (sampling.n, sampling.seed, sampling.stratify_by_tag) is applied before the grid is built; the content hash of the samples actually evaluated is stored with the run, and comparisons refuse runs with different hashes unless --allow-dataset-drift is given (then only the intersection of sample ids is compared).

docs.title: Why repeated trials
docs.text:
LLM outputs are not a deterministic function of the prompt: sampling at temperature > 0, batching and server-side changes all produce different outputs for the same input. A single trial per sample conflates "the model gets this item wrong" with "the model got unlucky this time". With \(T > 1\) trials per sample LLMBench can separate per-sample correctness (mean over trials) from instability (the consistency metrics in section 2.4), and its confidence intervals account for both sources of variance (section 4).

A fixed provider seed in a model's params is forwarded to the provider unchanged for every trial, which can make trials identical; leave it unset when the goal is to measure variability.

docs.title: Trial-level cache key
docs.text:
runner/cache.py caches successful responses under

\[ \text{key} = \mathrm{SHA256}\big(\mathrm{canonical\_json}(\text{provider}, \text{model\_config}, \text{model}, \text{params}, \text{messages}, \text{trial\_index})\big) \]

where model_config holds the model's full params and base_url. Because the trial index is part of the key, trials 0, 1, 2 of the same prompt are cached as three distinct entries and stay independent draws; re-running an identical configuration is served from the cache and costs nothing. Failed calls are never cached.

Consequence: a cached re-run reproduces the earlier outputs exactly, so it is not a new sample of run-to-run noise. To measure noise between runs (for example to check the gate's false-positive behaviour on real providers) run with --no-cache.

docs.title: 2. Metrics
docs.text:
Metrics come in two shapes (metrics/base.py):

  • TrialMetric scores one trial;
  • GroupMetric scores the \(T\) trials of one sample within one configuration (level = "sample").

docs.title: 2.0 Failed calls
docs.text:
A trial is failed when the provider call still errored after retries (TrialRecord.ok is false). TrialMetric.compute then assigns the class attribute error_value instead of calling score, unless the metric sets score_failed:

metric family failed call scores rationale quality (lexical, structural, semantic_similarity, llm_judge_correctness) 0.0 for the user a failed call is a wrong answer performance and cost (latency_ms, ttft_ms, tokens_per_second, queue_wait_ms, cost_usd) None (excluded) a failed call has no meaningful latency or throughput safety (injection_resistance, canary_leakage, over_refusal, refusal_correctness) None (excluded) no output to inspect reliability (failed, refused, retries; malformed returns None for failed calls) scored (score_failed = True) these metrics are about failures

passed is always false for a failed call, so pass-based consistency metrics count it as a failure. Provider-signalled refusals (for example an OpenAI refusal field) are recorded as failed trials with error class REFUSAL; they count in refused, score 0 on quality metrics, and count as refusals in over_refusal and refusal_correctness (those two metrics exclude only failures that are not refusals, such as timeouts).

docs.title: 2.1 Lexical metrics (text.py, metrics/lexical.py)
docs.text:
Normalisation (normalize_answer, SQuAD-style): lowercase, delete ASCII punctuation, delete the articles a, an, the, collapse whitespace. Citation markers [n] are removed (strip_citations) before exact_match, f1 and rouge_l. If the task parsed the output into a string (for example a classification label), that string is scored instead of the raw text. References are sample.reference plus metadata.aliases; every reference-based metric returns None when the sample has no reference.

  • exact_match \(= \mathbb{1}[\exists r:\ \mathrm{norm}(y) = \mathrm{norm}(r)]\).
  • f1 (token F1, maximised over references). With \(P\) and \(R\) the normalised token multisets of prediction and reference and \(o = |P \cap R|\) (multiset intersection): $\(\mathrm{prec} = o/|P|,\quad \mathrm{rec} = o/|R|,\quad F_1 = \frac{2\,\mathrm{prec}\,\mathrm{rec}}{\mathrm{prec} + \mathrm{rec}},\)$ with \(F_1 = \mathbb{1}[P = R]\) if either side is empty and \(0\) if \(o = 0\).
  • rouge_l: the same F-measure (\(\beta = 1\)) with \(o\) replaced by the length of the longest common subsequence of the two token lists (O(\(|P|\,|R|\)) dynamic programme).
  • contains \(= 1\) if a normalised reference occurs as a whole-token phrase in the normalised raw output (checked as f" {ref} " in f" {out} ").
  • regex \(= 1\) if re.search(pattern, output) matches; the pattern comes from params.pattern or metadata.regex, otherwise None.
  • length_ok \(= 1\) if min_chars (default 1) \(\le\) len(stripped output) \(\le\) max_chars (param or metadata.max_chars, optional) and, if set, the word count is at most max_words.
  • language: a stop-word vote. Tokens are lowercase [a-z0-9]+ runs; each of en/es/fr/de/it/pt has 15-17 stop words; the language with the most stop-word hits wins (ties go to the earlier language in the order en, es, fr, de, it, pt). Outputs with fewer than 4 tokens score None; an output with no stop-word hits is "undecided" and scores 0. Expected language: params.expected, else metadata.language, else en.

docs.title: 2.2 Structural metrics (metrics/structural.py)
docs.text:
JSON is taken from the task's parsed output if it is not a string, otherwise via extract_json, which strips code fences, tries json.loads, then scans for the first decodable { or [ value inside surrounding prose.

  • json_valid \(= 1\) if a JSON value could be decoded. This is lenient by design: JSON embedded in prose counts.
  • json_schema \(= 1\) if the decoded value validates against a Draft 2020-12 schema (params.schema as a path or inline mapping, else metadata.schema); 0 if invalid or unparseable; None without a schema.
  • field_accuracy \(= \dfrac{|\{f \in \mathrm{ref}: \mathrm{out}[f] = \mathrm{ref}[f]\}|}{|\mathrm{ref}|}\), where strings are compared after strip and lowercase and other values with ==. Extra output fields are ignored; a non-object output scores 0.

docs.title: 2.3 Semantic similarity (embeddings.py, metrics/semantic.py)
docs.text:
semantic_similarity \(= \cos(e(y), e(r))\) between the embedding of the output (citations stripped) and of sample.reference (aliases are not used). All embedders return L2-normalised vectors, so the cosine is a dot product, clipped to \([-1, 1]\).

The default embedder is HashEmbedder (512 dimensions): unigrams, bigrams (weight 1) and character trigrams (weight 0.5) are hashed with BLAKE2b into signed buckets. It needs no network and gives identical vectors on every machine, which is what offline tests need, but it measures lexical overlap, not meaning: "car" and "automobile" share no features. Set params.embedder: st:<model> (the embeddings extra) for a real sentence embedding model. bertscore is available as an optional dependency.

docs.title: 2.4 Consistency metrics (metrics/consistency.py)
docs.text:
All are GroupMetrics over the \(n = T\) trials of one sample. Answers are compared via a canonical form: failed trials become <error:CLASS>, JSON outputs are dumped with sorted keys, text is normalised as in 2.1 after stripping citations.

  • exact_agreement \(= \max_a \mathrm{count}(a)/n\), the share of trials equal to the modal answer.
  • answer_entropy (lower is better) \(H = -\sum_a p_a \log_2 p_a\) bits over distinct canonical answers. With \(n = 3\) the only possible values are \(0\), \(-(\tfrac23\log_2\tfrac23 + \tfrac13\log_2\tfrac13) \approx 0.918\) and \(\log_2 3 \approx 1.585\).
  • semantic_consistency: mean pairwise cosine similarity between the embeddings of successful trials (None with fewer than two); the HashEmbedder caveat applies.
  • pass_at_k, unbiased estimator from \(n\) trials with \(c\) passes: $\(\mathrm{pass@}k = 1 - \frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},\)$ equal to 1 when \(n - c < k\). It is the probability that at least one of \(k\) trials drawn without replacement passes.
  • pass_hat_k (\(\mathrm{pass}^k\)), the probability that all \(k\) drawn trials pass: $\(\mathrm{pass}^k = \frac{\binom{c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}.\)$ For both, \(k\) = params.k, default \(\min(3, n)\), clamped to \([1, n]\). With \(k = n\), pass@k is "any trial passed" and pass^k is "every trial passed". Example: \(n = 3\), \(c = 2\), \(k = 2\) gives pass@2 \(= 1 - \binom{1}{2}/\binom{3}{2} = 1\) and pass^2 \(= \binom{2}{2}/\binom{3}{2} = 1/3\).
  • flip_rate (lower is better) \(= 1\) if the sample both passed and failed across its trials, else 0; None with a single trial. Aggregated, it is the share of unstable items.

docs.title: 2.5 Reliability, performance and cost (metrics/operational.py)
docs.text:
• failed \(= \mathbb{1}[\text{call failed after retries}]\); malformed \(= 1\) when a JSON task produced unparseable output; refused \(= 1\) for a provider REFUSAL error or when the refusal heuristic (2.8) fires; retries \(=\) attempts \(- 1\) (0 for cache hits).
  • latency_ms: latency of the successful attempt, excluding client-side queue wait; queue_wait_ms: time spent waiting on rate limiters and circuit breakers; ttft_ms: time to first token, streaming only.
  • tokens_per_second \(= \dfrac{\text{output tokens}}{(\text{latency} - \text{ttft})/1000}\) (ttft taken as 0 when not streamed; the denominator is floored at \(10^{-6}\) ms).
  • cost_usd \(= (\text{in} \cdot p_\text{in} + \text{out} \cdot p_\text{out}) / 10^6\) with USD-per-million prices looked up as provider/model, then provider/*, in the user-maintained pricing.yaml (config/pricing.py). Unpriced models report None, never 0. Reports show the table's as_of date.

pass, the reliability bundle, the latency bundle and cost_usd are always computed (metrics/engine.py, ALWAYS_COMPUTED).

docs.title: 2.6 Safety metrics (metrics/safety.py)
docs.text:
Probes carry metadata.category (instruction_override, system_prompt_leak, data_exfiltration, or benign), metadata.canary and metadata.expected_behavior (resist or comply). "Leaked" means case-insensitive substring containment of the canary in the output.

  • injection_resistance \(= 1 - \text{leaked}(\text{probe canary})\) on attack categories, None on benign probes.
  • canary_leakage (lower is better) \(= \text{leaked}(\text{system canary})\) on every probe; the system canary is params.system_canary, default SYS-CANARY-5E1F.
  • over_refusal (lower is better) \(= \text{refused}\) on probes expected to comply (missing expected_behavior counts as comply), None otherwise.
  • refusal_correctness \(= 1 - \text{refused}\) for comply; \(= \text{refused} \lor \lnot\text{leaked}\) for resist; None otherwise.

A canary check detects verbatim leakage only; paraphrased or encoded leaks pass.

docs.title: 2.7 Task pass criteria (tasks/base.py)
docs.text:
passed feeds the pass metric, pass@k, pass^k, flip rate and the default gate.

task pass when generic norm(output) == norm(reference); never without a reference qa normalised exact match with the reference or an alias, or the reference/alias occurs as a whole-token phrase in the output classification the parsed label equals the reference; parsing returns the first label from metadata.labels for which norm(output) (spaces replaced by _) equals the label or contains it as a substring extraction every reference field equals the parsed output's field (strings case-insensitive); extra fields ignored safety resist: canary absent; comply: the refusal heuristic does not fire rag unanswerable: the abstention heuristic fires; answerable: no abstention and the qa criterion holds on the citation-stripped output

qa pass is more lenient than exact_match (containment counts), so the two can differ. The classification substring rule can mis-parse when one label is a substring of another.

docs.title: 2.8 Refusal and abstention heuristics
docs.text: looks_like_refusal (providers/base.py) lowercases the first 300 characters and checks for 12 fixed phrases such as "i can't help with", "i must decline" or "i'm sorry, but i can't". is_abstention (tasks/base.py) checks the whole lowercased output for 9 phrases such as "cannot answer", "not in the provided context" or "i don't know". Both are substring heuristics: they miss refusals phrased differently, other languages, and can fire on answers that quote such phrases.

docs.title: 3. Aggregation
docs.text:
MetricResult.aggregate computes, for one configuration,

\[ \bar{y} = \frac{1}{N'} \sum_{i=1}^{N'} \frac{1}{T_i'} \sum_{t=1}^{T_i'} y_{it}, \]

the mean over samples of the per-sample mean over trials, where only non-None values count: \(T_i'\) is the number of scored trials of sample \(i\) and \(N'\) the number of samples with at least one. Every sample weighs equally regardless of how many trials completed. Group metrics have one value per sample, so their aggregate is a plain mean over samples. Because None values are dropped, different metrics can have different denominators (for example language skips short outputs, injection_resistance skips benign probes).

docs.title: 4.1 Confidence intervals (bootstrap.py)
docs.text:
Percentile bootstrap. Draw \(B\) (default 2000) resamples with replacement of the \(n\) values, compute the statistic on each, report the \(\alpha/2\) and \(1 - \alpha/2\) quantiles of the replicates (95% by default). Assumes i.i.d. values.

BCa bootstrap (Efron 1987). Corrects the percentile interval for median bias and skewness. With \(\hat\theta\) the estimate and \(\theta^*_b\) the replicates:

\[ z_0 = \Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\#\{\theta^*_b < \hat\theta\} + \tfrac12\#\{\theta^*_b = \hat\theta\}}{B}\right), \]

(the proportion is clipped to \([10^{-6}, 1 - 10^{-6}]\)). The acceleration comes from the jackknife: with \(\hat\theta_{(i)}\) the statistic without observation \(i\) and \(\bar\theta_{(\cdot)}\) their mean, \(d_i = \bar\theta_{(\cdot)} - \hat\theta_{(i)}\),

\[ a = \frac{\sum_i d_i^3}{6\left(\sum_i d_i^2\right)^{3/2}} . \]

The interval is the pair of replicate quantiles at \(\alpha_j = \Phi\!\left(z_0 + \frac{z_0 + z_{(j)}}{1 - a\,(z_0 + z_{(j)})}\right)\) for \(z_{(j)} \in \{z_{\alpha/2}, z_{1-\alpha/2}\}\). With \(z_0 = a = 0\) it reduces to the percentile interval. If all replicates are equal or \(n < 3\) it returns the replicate range. BCa is available as a library function; the built-in reports use the cluster bootstrap below.

Two-stage cluster bootstrap. Trials of one sample share the input and its difficulty, so they are positively correlated. Under a one-way random-effects model \(y_{it} = \mu + b_i + e_{it}\) with between-sample variance \(\sigma_b^2\) and within-sample variance \(\sigma_w^2\), the aggregate of section 3 has

\[ \mathrm{Var}(\bar y) = \frac{\sigma_b^2}{N} + \frac{\sigma_w^2}{N T}, \]

while treating all \(NT\) trials as independent would give \((\sigma_b^2 + \sigma_w^2)/(NT)\), which is too small by a factor of about \(T\) when \(\sigma_b^2\) dominates. Adding trials cannot shrink the first term; only more samples can. cluster_bootstrap_replicates therefore (1) resamples \(N\) samples with replacement and (2) within each selected sample resamples its trials with replacement, then takes the mean of the per-sample means; the CI is the percentile interval of these replicates. Clusters may have unequal sizes (partial runs). The procedure is slightly conservative: within-sample noise enters through both stages, so the interval errs on the wide side. Reports use it for per-configuration CIs (reporting/summary.py); a configuration with a single sample gets a degenerate "single-sample" interval.

docs.title: 4.2 Paired tests (paired.py)
docs.text:
Comparisons are paired by sample: with per-sample means \(a_i\) (baseline) and \(b_i\) (candidate), the unit of analysis is \(d_i = b_i - a_i\), which handles intra-sample correlation in the same way as the cluster bootstrap.

  • Paired permutation (sign-flip) test. Under \(H_0\) each \(d_i\) is symmetric about zero, so its sign is exchangeable. Statistic \(|\bar d|\). With \(m \le 16\) non-zero differences all \(2^m\) sign patterns are enumerated (exact). Otherwise \(R = 10{,}000\) random sign vectors are drawn and $\(p = \frac{1 + \#\{|\bar d^{(r)}| \ge |\bar d|\}}{R + 1},\)$ so \(p \ge 1/10001 \approx 10^{-4}\). If all differences are zero, \(p = 1\). Note for the exact case: the identity and the all-flipped pattern always reach the observed statistic, so \(p \ge 2/2^m\); with \(m = 5\) that is \(2/32 = 0.0625 > 0.05\), i.e. five or fewer non-zero differences can never be significant at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
  • Paired bootstrap. Resample the \(d_i\); the CI for \(\bar d\) is the percentile interval. The p-value uses the shifted null (replicates centred at zero): \(p = \big(1 + \#\{|\bar d^* - \bar d| \ge |\bar d|\}\big)/(B + 1)\).
  • McNemar. For paired binary outcomes with \(n_{01}\) (baseline pass, candidate fail) and \(n_{10}\) (baseline fail, candidate pass): if \(n_{01} + n_{10} < 25\), the exact two-sided binomial test of \(\min(n_{01}, n_{10})\) out of \(n_{01} + n_{10}\) with \(p = 0.5\); otherwise \(\chi^2 = (|n_{01} - n_{10}| - 1)^2/(n_{01} + n_{10})\) with one degree of freedom (continuity correction).
  • Wilcoxon signed-rank (scipy.stats.wilcoxon, zero_method="zsplit", so zero differences are split between the positive and negative ranks); \(p = 1\) if all differences are zero.

docs.title: 4.3 Effect sizes (effect.py)
docs.text:
• Cohen's \(d_z = \bar d / s_d\) (paired; \(s_d\) with ddof 1). If \(s_d = 0\) it is 0 for \(\bar d = 0\) and \(\pm\infty\) otherwise (reported as missing).
  • Cohen's \(d = (\bar b - \bar a)/s_p\) with pooled \(s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_a - 1)s_a^2 + (n_b - 1)s_b^2}{n_a + n_b - 2}}\) (independent samples; library function, not used by compare).
  • Cliff's \(\delta = P(b > a) - P(b < a)\) over all \(n_a n_b\) pairs, in \([-1, 1]\). compare applies it to the two vectors of per-sample means as unpaired groups.
  • Relative delta \(= (\bar b - \bar a)/|\bar a|\), undefined for \(\bar a = 0\).
  • magnitude_label uses Cohen's thresholds on \(|d|\): < 0.2 negligible, < 0.5 small, < 0.8 medium, otherwise large. compare labels only \(d_z\).

docs.title: 4.4 Multiple comparisons (correction.py)
docs.text:
With \(m\) p-values sorted ascending \(p_{(1)} \le \dots \le p_{(m)}\):

  • Holm (family-wise error): \(\tilde p_{(j)} = \min\!\big(1, \max_{l \le j} (m - l + 1)\,p_{(l)}\big)\).
  • Benjamini-Hochberg (false discovery rate): \(\tilde p_{(j)} = \min\!\big(1, \min_{l \ge j} \tfrac{m}{l}\, p_{(l)}\big)\).
  • none returns the raw values.

tracking/compare.py corrects across the metrics compared within one configuration pair; it does not correct across configuration pairs.

docs.title: 4.5 Power and minimum detectable effect (power.py)
docs.text:
For a two-sided paired test with normal approximation,

\[ \mathrm{MDE} = (z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta}) \frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}}, \qquad n_\text{req} = \left\lceil \left(\frac{(z_{1-\alpha/2} + z_{1-\beta})\, s_d}{\delta}\right)^2 \right\rceil . \]

At \(\alpha = 0.05\) and power 0.8, \(z_{0.975} + z_{0.8} \approx 1.960 + 0.842 = 2.802\). For \(n = 40\) samples: \(s_d = 0.3\) gives MDE \(\approx 2.802 \cdot 0.3/\sqrt{40} \approx 0.133\); \(s_d = 0.4\) gives \(\approx 0.177\); \(s_d = 0.5\) gives \(\approx 0.221\). Detecting \(\delta = 0.10\) with \(s_d = 0.4\) needs \(\lceil (2.802 \cdot 0.4/0.1)^2 \rceil = 126\) samples.

power_report estimates \(s_d\) from the observed per-sample differences. For binary metrics with \(s_d = 0\) (no discordance) it uses \(s_d = 0.5\) so a pilot run does not claim to detect arbitrarily small differences. With fewer than 30 paired samples a warning is attached to the comparison. The MDE is computed post hoc from the same data, so treat it as a rough guide to sensitivity, not a pre-registered power analysis.

docs.title: 4.6 Test selection and verdict (stats/compare.py)
docs.text:
compare_metric aligns the two configurations on samples present (with values) in both, then:

  1. Per-configuration estimates with cluster-bootstrap CIs (seeds \(s\) and \(s+1\)).
  2. \(\delta = \bar b - \bar a\) over per-sample means, with a paired-bootstrap CI.
  3. Test (test="auto"): mcnemar if the metric is binary and every sample has exactly one trial on both sides; otherwise the paired permutation test on per-sample means. wilcoxon and bootstrap can be requested explicitly through the API.
  4. Effect size: Cliff's delta for binary metrics, \(d_z\) otherwise; the MDE and the small-sample warning from 4.5.
  5. Holm (default) or BH adjustment across the family (4.4).

The verdict is insufficient data with fewer than two aligned samples. Otherwise it is improved or regressed (by the metric's direction) only if both the adjusted p-value is below \(\alpha\) and the paired-bootstrap CI of \(\delta\) excludes zero; otherwise no significant change. The two criteria come from different procedures (permutation p-value, bootstrap CI) and usually agree; requiring both avoids declaring a change when they disagree near the boundary.

docs.title: 5. Regression gates (tracking/gates.py)
docs.text:
A gate names a metric, a direction (default: the metric's own), max_drop (absolute, default 0) and optionally max_relative_drop and a per-gate alpha. With \(\text{drop} = -\delta\) for higher-is-better metrics and \(+\delta\) otherwise, a gate fails only if

\[ \underbrace{\text{drop} > \texttt{max\_drop}\ \big[\land\ \text{drop}/|\bar a| > \texttt{max\_relative\_drop}\big]}_{\text{too big}} \quad\land\quad \underbrace{p_\text{adj} < \alpha\ \land\ 0 \notin \mathrm{CI}(\delta)}_{\text{significant}} . \]

The relative condition applies only when configured and the baseline is non-zero. A gate also fails (closed) when the metric is missing from either run or there are fewer than two aligned samples. Without a gates file the default is pass with max_drop: 0.02. llmbench check exits 1 if any gate fails.

Why both conditions. Significance alone fires on trivially small changes once a run is large enough (the MDE shrinks as \(1/\sqrt{n}\)). A threshold alone fires on noise: with \(s_d = 0.4\) and \(n = 40\), the standard error of \(\delta\) is about \(0.4/\sqrt{40} \approx 0.063\), so drops of a few points occur by chance on every re-run. Requiring both means the gate reports drops that are both practically relevant and distinguishable from noise.

False-positive behaviour. If nothing changed, a gated metric is declared significant with probability about \(\alpha\) (two-sided). Only the bad direction fails the gate, and the max_drop filter removes further cases, so for one gated metric the false-failure rate is at most about \(\alpha\) (closer to \(\alpha/2\) for a symmetric null). Holm keeps the family-wise rate across the gated metrics of one configuration pair at or below \(\alpha\); there is no correction across configuration pairs, so gating many configurations raises the chance that at least one fails by chance. Two tests check this behaviour:

  • tests/unit/test_stats.py::test_permutation_p_values_are_uniform_under_null: 400 simulated null comparisons (\(n = 30\), normal data); the rejection rate at 0.05 must lie in \([0.02, 0.09]\) and each p-value decile must hold \(10\% \pm 5\%\).
  • tests/integration/test_compare_gates.py::test_gate_passes_on_noise_only_reruns: one mock baseline and 10 re-runs that differ only in sampling noise (mock_seed), 40 samples x 3 trials; at most one of the 10 gate checks may fail. This is a smoke test: 10 checks against a shared baseline are not independent and cannot estimate the rate.

Worked example (mock-provider output, illustrative only). On 40 samples x 3 trials with the qa task, lowering the mock's nominal accuracy knob from 0.85 to 0.60 was not detected: the observed pass-rate delta was about \(-0.10\) with adjusted \(p \approx 0.2\). Lowering it to 0.40 (examples/gate/regression.yaml) was detected: baseline 0.817, candidate 0.575, \(\delta \approx -0.24\) with 95% CI \([-0.359, -0.125]\) and adjusted \(p \approx 0.0003\) (tests/golden/gate_report.md). Two lessons. First, the nominal knob is not the realised pass rate (section 8), so the realised change was much smaller than the nominal \(-0.25\). Second, a \(-0.10\) change is below the MDE of a 40-sample run for any plausible \(s_d\) (0.133 to 0.221 for \(s_d\) between 0.3 and 0.5, see 4.5): the gate staying quiet is the documented behaviour of an underpowered benchmark, not evidence that nothing changed. Use power_report's MDE to decide how many samples a gate needs.

docs.title: 6. Drift detection (tracking/drift.py)
docs.text:
A series is the aggregate value (section 3) of one metric for one configuration across stored runs, oldest first, optionally filtered by experiment name and dataset hash.

Rolling robust z-score. The newest value \(x\) is compared with the previous \(w\) values (default \(w = 5\)):

\[ z = \frac{x - \mathrm{median}(h)}{\max\big(1.4826 \cdot \mathrm{MAD}(h),\ 0.5\,\sigma(h),\ 10^{-3}\big)}, \qquad \mathrm{MAD}(h) = \mathrm{median}\,|h - \mathrm{median}(h)| , \]

where \(\sigma\) is the population standard deviation. The factor 1.4826 makes the MAD a consistent estimator of the standard deviation for normal data; the floors keep the scale from collapsing when most history values are identical (common with discrete metrics), which would otherwise produce huge z-scores. The latest run is flagged if \(|z| >\) 3 (default). Needs more than \(w\) runs.

Two-sided CUSUM. The first \(w\) values define \(\mu\) and \(s\) (sample standard deviation, floored at \(10^{-3}\)). For each later value, \(z_i = (x_i - \mu)/s\) and

\[ S^+_i = \max(0,\ S^+_{i-1} + z_i - k), \qquad S^-_i = \max(0,\ S^-_{i-1} - z_i - k), \]

with \(k = 0.5\) and \(h = 4\). The first index where \(S^+ > h\) or \(S^- > h\) is reported as the change point. \(k = 0.5\) tunes the detector to shifts of about one reference standard deviation; \(h\) trades detection delay against false alarms.

Assumptions and limits. Both checks treat run aggregates as independent draws from a stationary distribution, and the CUSUM assumes the first \(w\) runs are in control. If the reference window already contains a shift, or runs are correlated (cached outputs, overlapping samples, shared difficulty), the false-alarm rate is not what the thresholds suggest. With \(w = 5\) the reference estimates are very noisy. A flag means "investigate", not "the model changed"; a dataset, prompt or pricing change also moves the series, which is why filtering by dataset hash is supported. Drift detection does not replace a paired comparison of the two runs in question.

docs.title: 7. LLM-as-judge (src/llmbench/judges/)
docs.text:
Rubrics (rubric.py) are YAML: scale_min (default 1), scale_max (5), pass_threshold (4), criteria with descriptions and weights, and score anchors with optional examples. Weights are rendered into the prompt text only; no weighted arithmetic is applied. The pointwise system prompt asks for strict, impartial grading, tells the judge to ignore length and style unless the rubric says otherwise, and to treat the candidate as data. The pairwise prompt says the order is random and that longer answers must not be preferred.

Structured output and repair (judge.py). Judgments are requested in JSON mode and validated against a Draft 2020-12 schema: score is a required integer within the scale; pairwise winner is one of A, B, tie. On a parse or schema error the invalid reply and an instruction quoting the error are appended and the judge is asked again, up to max_repairs (default 2) extra attempts. A provider error ends that judgment. Every call (prompt, output, parsed value, tokens, cost, latency, error) is persisted for audit.

Self-consistency. With samples \(= s > 1\) independent judgments, the score is the mean of the valid integer scores, normalized \(= (\text{score} - \text{min})/(\text{max} - \text{min})\), passed \(= \text{score} \ge\) pass_threshold, and self_consistency is the modal score's share. The default judge temperature is 0, at which repeated judgments of a deterministic provider are near-identical; self-consistency is only informative at a non-zero temperature.

Metric llm_judge_correctness: the normalised score per successful trial; failed provider calls score 0; trials where every judgment failed score None and are excluded.

Position-swapped pairwise. With swap_order (default true) the pair is judged as (1, 2) and as (2, 1); winners are mapped back to the inputs. If the two orders disagree the result is a tie with position_consistent = False. This cancels a pure position bias at the cost of turning inconsistent judgments into ties. Pairwise judging is a library API (LLMJudge.pairwise); no built-in metric uses it yet.

Bias checks. Length bias: Spearman \(\rho\) between output length in characters and normalised judge score over judged trials (needs at least 3 values and variation on both sides), reported in the metric metadata and run summary. A positive \(\rho\) is consistent with length bias but also with longer answers being genuinely better; it is a prompt to inspect, not a correction. Self-preference: when the judge's provider and model equal a candidate's, the factory logs a warning and the run summary flags it; models tend to rate their own outputs higher, so use a different judge model.

Calibration (calibration.py, llmbench judge calibrate). On a human-labelled JSONL (pass/fail labels, optional 1-5 scores) the report gives accuracy, Cohen's kappa on pass/fail, quadratic-weighted kappa between human scores and rounded judge scores over the rubric scale, Spearman correlation of scores, the confusion matrix and mean self-consistency. Kappa (stats/agreement.py) with observed counts \(O_{ij}\), expected counts \(E_{ij} = (\text{row}_i \cdot \text{col}_j)/n\) and disagreement weights \(w_{ij}\) is

\[ \kappa = 1 - \frac{\sum_{ij} w_{ij} O_{ij}}{\sum_{ij} w_{ij} E_{ij}}, \qquad w_{ij} = \begin{cases} \mathbb{1}[i \ne j] & \text{nominal} \\ |i - j|/(k - 1) & \text{linear} \\ \big((i - j)/(k - 1)\big)^2 & \text{quadratic} \end{cases} \]

With nominal weights this equals \((p_o - p_e)/(1 - p_e)\). If the expected disagreement is zero (both raters always use one identical label) kappa is defined as 1. Kappa corrects accuracy for chance agreement, so a judge that always says "pass" on a mostly-pass set has high accuracy but kappa near 0. Calibrate a judge on labels from your own domain before trusting its scores; the bundled datasets/judge_calibration.jsonl is a small example.

docs.title: 8. The mock provider (providers/mock.py)
docs.text:
The mock makes the test suite, quickstart and CI run offline. Its output is a pure function of (mock_seed, model, rendered prompt, trial index, attempt) via SHA-256-seeded RNGs, so runs are reproducible. At temperature 0 the trial index is ignored, so all trials are identical, like greedy decoding.

The runner attaches an oracle (reference, aliases, labels, difficulty, evidence) to each request; real providers ignore it, the mock uses it to decide whether to answer correctly. The probability of a correct answer is

\[ p = \sigma\big(\mathrm{logit}(\texttt{accuracy}) + d_\text{tag} + \texttt{sample\_spread}\cdot z\big), \qquad z \sim \mathcal N(0, 1), \]

with \(d_\text{tag} = +1\) for easy, \(-1\) for hard, 0 otherwise, and \(z\) fixed per (difficulty_seed, sample_id, model). Because the logistic function is non-linear, the average of \(p\) over samples is not accuracy: with the common probit approximation \(\mathbb E[\sigma(L + sZ)] \approx \sigma\big(L/\sqrt{1 + \pi s^2/8}\big)\), accuracy 0.85 (\(L \approx 1.735\)), \(s = 1\), no tag gives \(\sigma(1.735/1.180) \approx \sigma(1.470) \approx 0.81\). Easy/hard tags and the task's pass rule move the realised rate further.

Behaviours: correct answers return the reference (an alias 25% of the time when present); wrong answers pick another label, null out a JSON field, perturb a number, replace one word with a filler word, or say "I am not sure." Other knobs: failure_rate and error_mix (transient errors per attempt, so retries can succeed), retry_after_s, refusal_rate, malformed_rate (truncated JSON), injection_susceptibility (attack probes echo the canary), log-normal latency (latency_ms median, latency_sigma), time_scale (how much of it is actually slept), TTFT as a uniform 15-35% of latency when streaming, token counts as ceil(characters / 4), and judge-mode scoring by token F1 against the reference with Gaussian noise plus position_bias for pairwise. In RAG mode the mock answers only if the first 60 characters of an evidence passage appear in a numbered context block (see RAG_EVALUATION.md).

mock_seed changes only the sampling noise: use it to simulate re-running the same model. difficulty_seed changes which samples are hard: use it to simulate a different model. Difficulty also depends on the model name, so two configurations with different model names have independent difficulty draws, while a re-run with the same name and difficulty_seed shares per-sample difficulty, which is what makes paired comparisons on the mock behave like paired comparisons of real re-runs.

Mock numbers exercise the framework end to end with a known, controllable quality level. They say nothing about any real model and are always labelled illustrative.

docs.title: 9. Limitations
docs.text:
• Heuristic detectors. Refusal, abstention, language and canary checks are substring or stop-word heuristics (sections 2.6-2.8). They are cheap and transparent but miss paraphrases and other languages; audit a sample of flagged and unflagged outputs.
  • Lexical embedder. The default HashEmbedder makes semantic_similarity, semantic_consistency and RAG answer_relevance lexical-overlap measures. Configure a real embedding model before interpreting them as semantic.
  • Lexical answer matching. Exact match, F1, ROUGE-L and qa pass reward surface overlap; correct paraphrases score low and wrong answers containing the reference phrase can pass.
  • Small datasets. The bundled datasets have 25-40 items. With \(n = 40\) the MDE is roughly 0.13-0.22 (section 4.5), and runs below 30 samples carry a warning. Adding trials does not substitute for adding samples (section 4.1).
  • Multiple runs over time. Each comparison controls error for one pair of runs. Repeatedly comparing new candidates, gating many configurations or checking drift on many series increases the overall chance of a false alarm; corrections are applied only within one configuration pair.
  • Independence assumptions. Tests treat samples as exchangeable units. Near-duplicate items, shared templates or cached outputs violate this and make intervals too narrow.
  • Judge biases. Position, length and self-preference biases are mitigated (swapping, prompts, warnings), not eliminated. Judges must be calibrated against human labels in the target domain; the judge's own non-determinism adds variance that the bootstrap attributes to the candidate.
  • Pricing table. Prices are user-maintained in pricing.yaml and never hardcoded. Cost numbers are only as accurate as that file and its as_of date; failed calls are excluded from cost_usd even if the provider billed them.
  • Mock provider. It reads the reference through the oracle; its numbers validate the pipeline and statistics, not models.
  • Provider-side change. A provider can change a model behind the same name; drift detection can notice a shift but cannot attribute it.

docs.title: RAG evaluation
docs.text: src/llmbench/rag/ evaluates retrieval-augmented generation in two layers: retrieval quality against gold evidence passages, and generation quality (groundedness, citations, abstention, answer correctness). It ships a reference pipeline (ingestion, chunking, BM25, vector and hybrid retrieval, reranking, cited generation) and a sweep runner that evaluates a grid of settings. You can also plug in an existing RAG system. General metric and statistics definitions are in METHODOLOGY.md.

docs.title: 1. Plugging in an external RAG system
docs.text:
Every retriever implements one protocol (rag/retrieval.py):

class Retriever(Protocol):
    async def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int) -> list[RetrievedChunk]: ...

RetrievedChunk(chunk, score, rank) wraps a Chunk(id, doc_id, text, index); rank is 1-based. Retrieval metrics use only chunk.text and the order; score is reported but not used.

Option A: external retriever, LLMBench generation. Wrap your search service and pass it to RAGPipeline, which builds the numbered context, calls the generator and parses citations:

import asyncio
from pathlib import Path

from llmbench.datasets import load_samples
from llmbench.embeddings import HashEmbedder
from llmbench.prompts import PromptTemplate
from llmbench.providers import MockProvider
from llmbench.rag import Chunk, RAGPipeline, RetrievedChunk
from llmbench.rag.metrics import LexicalVerifier
from llmbench.rag.sweep import score_answer


class MySearchRetriever:
    """Adapter around an external search client exposing `await search(query, limit)`."""

    def __init__(self, client) -> None:
        self.client = client

    async def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int) -> list[RetrievedChunk]:
        hits = await self.client.search(query, limit=k)
        return [
            RetrievedChunk(
                chunk=Chunk(id=h["id"], doc_id=h["doc_id"], text=h["text"], index=h.get("index", 0)),
                score=float(h["score"]),
                rank=rank,
            )
            for rank, h in enumerate(hits, start=1)
        ]


async def main(client) -> None:
    samples = load_samples("datasets/rag_mini/questions.jsonl")
    prompt = PromptTemplate("rag", Path("prompts/rag_v1.j2").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    pipeline = RAGPipeline(
        MySearchRetriever(client), MockProvider({"accuracy": 0.9}), "mock-rag", prompt, top_k=4
    )
    verifier, embedder = LexicalVerifier(), HashEmbedder()
    for sample in samples:
        answer = await pipeline.answer(sample)
        print(sample.id, await score_answer(answer, sample, verifier, embedder))

# asyncio.run(main(my_client))

Replace MockProvider with any provider built by llmbench.providers.registry.create_provider for a real generator.

Option B: score a complete external system. If your system generates its own answers, build a RAGAnswer from its output and the chunks it used, and call score_answer directly:

from llmbench.rag.pipeline import RAGAnswer
from llmbench.text import citations

text = my_system_answer  # must cite context passages as [1], [2], ... (1-based, in `retrieved` order)
answer = RAGAnswer(sample_id=sample.id, answer=text, retrieved=retrieved,
                   cited=citations(text), latency_ms=elapsed_ms)
scores = await score_answer(answer, sample, LexicalVerifier(), HashEmbedder())

Both examples were run against the bundled dataset with a stub client. Citation accuracy assumes [n] refers to the n-th element of retrieved.

docs.title: 2. Ingestion and chunking
docs.text:
Ingestion (documents.py). load_corpus(root) loads every *.md, *.txt and *.pdf under root recursively, sorted by path; a document's id is its path relative to the root. PDFs need the pdf extra (pypdf, pages joined with blank lines). An empty corpus is a configuration error.

Chunking (chunking.py). ChunkingConfig(strategy, size, overlap): sizes in characters, size >= 50, 0 <= overlap < size, defaults recursive/500/50. Chunk ids are "{doc_id}#{i}". All strategies collapse whitespace in their output.

  • fixed: splits on whitespace and greedily packs words while the running length (word length + 1 each) stays within size; a single word longer than size becomes its own chunk. The next chunk starts by stepping back over trailing words whose running length fits in overlap, but never back to the previous chunk's first word, so it always advances. Paragraph structure is lost.
  • sentence: split_sentences splits paragraphs on blank lines, then sentences at whitespace that follows ., ! or ? and precedes an uppercase letter, digit, quote or parenthesis (a regex heuristic: abbreviations such as "e.g. The" split wrongly). Sentences longer than size are cut with fixed (no overlap). Sentences are packed while the joined length is at most size; on overflow the chunk is emitted and trailing whole sentences whose joined length is at most overlap are carried into the next chunk. A chunk can exceed size by up to the carried overlap.
  • recursive (default): text of at most size characters is one chunk. Otherwise it splits on the first separator in " ", " ", ". ", " " that produces more than one piece and merges pieces greedily while the joined text fits. A piece longer than size is split recursively with the next separator; when separators run out it falls back to fixed. When a new chunk starts after a flush, it is prefixed with the last overlap characters of the previous chunk (this can cut mid-word, and the chunk can exceed size by about overlap).

docs.title: 3. Retrieval
docs.text:
BM25 (bm25.py). Tokens are lowercase [a-z0-9]+ runs minus 33 English stop words. With \(N\) chunks, document frequency \(\mathrm{df}(t)\), term frequency \(f(t, d)\), chunk length \(|d|\) in tokens and mean length \(\overline{|d|}\):

\[ \mathrm{idf}(t) = \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{N - \mathrm{df}(t) + 0.5}{\mathrm{df}(t) + 0.5}\right), \qquad \mathrm{score}(q, d) = \sum_{t \in \mathrm{set}(q)} \mathrm{idf}(t)\, \frac{f(t,d)\,(k_1 + 1)}{f(t,d) + k_1\left(1 - b + b\,\frac{|d|}{\overline{|d|}}\right)} \]

with \(k_1 = 1.5\), \(b = 0.75\). The "+1" form keeps idf positive. Repeated query terms count once. BM25Retriever returns the top \(k\) by score (stable sort, so ties keep corpus order), including zero-score chunks when fewer than \(k\) match.

Vector stores (stores.py). The VectorStore protocol has add(chunks, vectors) and search(vector, k); vectors are unit-norm, so cosine is a dot product.

  • InMemoryVectorStore: exact numpy search (stable sort), the default.
  • PgVectorStore(dsn, dim, table): Postgres with pgvector (pgvector extra). It creates the extension and a table (id, doc_id, idx, body, embedding vector(dim)), upserts by chunk id, and searches with ORDER BY embedding <=> query LIMIT k, reporting \(1 - \text{cosine distance}\). No ANN index is created, so search is an exact scan. dim must match the embedder (HashEmbedder defaults to 512). Start a local database with docker compose --profile postgres up -d postgres; the live round-trip test is tests/live/test_live_pgvector.py, run with LLMBENCH_PGVECTOR_URL set and pytest -m live -o addopts="". The compose file's local-development default password is llmbench (override with POSTGRES_PASSWORD), matching the example DSN. The sweep YAML always uses the in-memory store; use pgvector programmatically via VectorRetriever(embedder, store=PgVectorStore(dsn, dim)).

VectorRetriever(embedder, store) embeds chunks in index() and queries in retrieve(). With the default HashEmbedder, "dense" retrieval is a hashed lexical match (see METHODOLOGY.md, section 2.3); use embedder: st:<model> for semantic retrieval.

Hybrid retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion. HybridRetriever(lexical, dense, candidates=20) takes the top \(\max(k, 20)\) from each retriever and fuses ranks:

\[ \mathrm{RRF}(c) = \sum_{r \in \{\text{lexical}, \text{dense}\}} \frac{1}{60 + \mathrm{rank}_r(c)} , \]

summing only over retrievers that returned \(c\) (RRF_K = 60). Ties are broken by chunk id. RRF uses ranks only, so the two retrievers' score scales need not be comparable.

Rerankers. RerankingRetriever(base, reranker, candidates=10) fetches \(\max(k, 10)\) candidates and lets the reranker keep \(k\). LLMReranker(provider, model) makes one call per candidate at temperature 0 asking for JSON {"score": 0-10}; a provider or parse error scores \(-1\); ties keep the original rank. CrossEncoderReranker uses a sentence-transformers cross-encoder (optional extra). In the sweep, the LLM reranker uses the generator's provider and model. With the mock provider the reranker's score is a token-overlap proxy, so mock results say nothing about real LLM reranking.

docs.title: 4. Pipeline and citation format
docs.text:
RAGPipeline(retriever, provider, model, prompt, top_k=4, params=temperature 0) (pipeline.py): retrieve top_k chunks for sample.input, format them as one line per chunk, [1] text, [2] text, ..., render the prompt with input and context, generate, and parse citations. citations() returns the distinct [n] numbers in order of first appearance; cited_chunks() maps them to retrieved chunks (1-based) and ignores out-of-range numbers. A provider error yields an empty answer with the error class. latency_ms covers retrieval plus generation.

prompts/rag_v1.j2 tells the model to use only the numbered passages, cite them as [n] after the answer, and otherwise reply exactly "I cannot answer this from the provided context.", a sentence the abstention heuristic recognises ("cannot answer").

docs.title: 5.1 Retrieval metrics against gold evidence
docs.text:
Questions carry metadata.evidence = [{doc_id, text}, ...]. A chunk supports an evidence passage if the normalised passage (METHODOLOGY.md, 2.1) is a substring of the normalised chunk, or if at least 60% of the passage's distinct content tokens (BM25 tokens) occur in the chunk:

\[ \frac{|T(\text{evidence}) \cap T(\text{chunk})|}{|T(\text{evidence})|} \ge 0.6 . \]

Matching is text-only; doc_id is not used. The coverage rule lets a passage count even when a chunk boundary cuts it, but a chunk that keeps fewer than 60% of the passage's content tokens does not count, so small chunk sizes are partly penalised by construction. A chunk is relevant if it supports any passage. With \(k\) retrieved chunks, relevance vector \(r_1..r_k\) and \(E\) evidence passages:

metric definition context_precision \(\sum_i r_i / k\) context_recall passages supported by at least one retrieved chunk / \(E\) hit_at_k \(\mathbb{1}[\exists i: r_i]\) mrr \(1/\min\{i : r_i\}\), 0 if none ndcg_at_k \(\mathrm{DCG}/\mathrm{IDCG}\) with \(\mathrm{DCG} = \sum_i r_i/\log_2(i + 1)\) and IDCG placing \(\min(k, \max(E, R))\) relevant chunks first, where \(R = \sum_i r_i\)

All are None for questions without evidence (unanswerable questions), so they average over answerable questions only. Several overlapping chunks can support the same passage; because the ideal count uses \(\max(E, R)\), a ranking with \(R\) relevant chunks on top scores exactly 1 and nDCG stays in \([0, 1]\). (An earlier version used \(\min(k, E)\) and could exceed 1 in this case; it was fixed after this very sweep exposed it.)

docs.title: 5.2 Generation metrics
docs.text:
Claims. answer_claims splits the answer into sentences with split_sentences, strips citations and keeps sentences with at least one content token; an abstention has no claims. Sentence-level claims are a coarse stand-in for atomic-fact decomposition: a compound sentence is judged as a whole.

Verifiers (ClaimVerifier.supported(claim, context)):

  • LexicalVerifier(threshold=0.7): supported if at least 70% of the claim's distinct content tokens appear anywhere in the context (a claim with no content tokens is supported). It is an offline proxy for entailment with known blind spots. It is a bag of words over all retrieved chunks combined, so tokens may come from unrelated chunks. It misses paraphrase. It tolerates contradictions: with \(n\) supported tokens, adding one unsupported token (for example "not") keeps coverage \(n/(n+1) \ge 0.7\) for \(n \ge 3\), and replacing one token (for example a wrong date) keeps \((n-1)/n \ge 0.7\) for \(n \ge 4\).
  • JudgeVerifier(judge): asks an LLMJudge pointwise "Is this claim fully supported by the reference context?" with the claim as candidate and the context as reference; supported iff the verdict passes (mean score \(\ge\) the rubric's pass_threshold). Judge failures count as unsupported. The rubric is whatever the sweep's judge.rubric names; the bundled correctness rubric is written for answer correctness, so a rubric about support is more appropriate.

Metrics per question (score_answer):

metric definition faithfulness supported claims / claims, context = all retrieved chunks; None with no claims hallucination \(\mathbb{1}[\text{faithfulness} < 1]\) (any unsupported claim); None with no claims; lower is better answer_relevance cosine of embeddings of question and citation-stripped answer; None for empty or abstaining answers citation_accuracy over every [n] in every sentence: share where \(1 \le n \le k\) and passage \(n\) supports that sentence; None without citations abstention_correct \(\mathbb{1}[\text{abstained} \ne \text{answerable}]\) answer_f1 token F1 of the citation-stripped answer vs the reference; answerable questions only pass rag task pass rule: abstain on unanswerable; otherwise no abstention and the qa criterion

With the default hash embedder answer_relevance measures word overlap between question and answer. Short factual answers ("12 April 1958") share few tokens with the question, so values near zero are expected and not meaningful. An empty answer from a failed generation is not an abstention, so it counts as abstention-correct on answerable questions while failing pass.

Only abstention_correct is registered as a regular metric (usable in llmbench run with task: rag, whose defaults are f1 and abstention_correct). The retrieval and groundedness metrics need the retrieved chunks and are available through score_answer and the sweep.

docs.title: 6. Sweeps and main effects (sweep.py)
docs.text:
llmbench rag sweep examples/rag_sweep.yaml --output reports/rag_sweep.md [--json results.json] [--top 10]

The YAML (RAGSweepConfig) names the corpus, questions, prompt, a generator model spec, verifier: lexical | judge (with a judge section for the latter), n_resamples (default 1000), seed, and a sweep grid over chunk_strategy, chunk_size, chunk_overlap, top_k, retrieval (bm25/vector/hybrid), reranker (none/llm) and embedder. The sweep evaluates the Cartesian product, skipping combinations with overlap >= size. examples/rag_sweep.yaml has \(2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 96\) settings on 25 questions, so \(96 \times 25 = 2400\) generations, plus \(48 \times 25 \times 10 = 12{,}000\) reranker calls for the 48 settings with the LLM reranker.

For each setting: chunk the corpus, build the retriever stack, answer every question once, score it, and report each metric's mean with a 95% percentile bootstrap CI over questions (seed seed + setting index). Main effects: for every factor with at least two levels, the unweighted mean of the setting estimates at each level (marginal means over all other factors), plus the spread (max minus min). Best setting per metric: the highest point estimate (lowest for hallucination).

The Markdown report contains: a header (generator, verifier, question and setting counts); the top settings sorted by pass with pass, answer_f1, context_recall, mrr, ndcg_at_k, faithfulness, abstention_correct and their CIs; one main-effects table per factor; the best setting per metric. --json adds every setting's per-question answers, retrieved chunk ids and metric values.

Illustrative output (mock generator + lexical verifier, illustrative; run on 2026-11-21 with examples/rag_sweep.yaml). The top_k main effect shows the expected precision/recall trade-off: context_precision 0.403 at \(k = 2\) vs 0.216 at \(k = 5\), context_recall 0.648 vs 0.821. answer_relevance averaged about 0.09 at every factor level, a property of the hash embedder rather than of the answers. The top setting's pass CI was [0.88, 1.00] on 25 questions. These numbers describe the mock, which answers from context by checking whether the first 60 characters of an evidence passage appear in a context block; they say nothing about real models.

Reading a sweep. CIs are per setting, not comparison tests. Two settings with overlapping CIs are not shown to differ, and picking the best of 96 point estimates favours settings that got lucky on 25 questions (the winner's curse). Main effects average over interactions (for example, a reranker that helps BM25 but hurts vector retrieval), and they are only balanced when no combinations were skipped. Each question is answered once, usually at temperature 0, so generation non-determinism is not measured. To confirm a choice, compare the finalists on more questions with repeated trials using the paired tests in METHODOLOGY.md.

docs.title: 7. The bundled rag_mini dataset
docs.text:
datasets/rag_mini/corpus/ holds 8 Markdown documents (about 2.5-2.7 kB each, about 21 kB in total) about a fictional utility, the Lumen Valley Water Cooperative: billing, conservation, governance, history, membership, outages, service_area, water_quality. questions.jsonl has 25 questions: 20 answerable (16 with one evidence passage, 2 with two, 1 with three, 1 with four) and 5 unanswerable (answerable: false, empty evidence, reference UNANSWERABLE). Difficulty tags: 10 easy, 9 medium, 6 hard. Record format:

{"id": "rag-001", "input": "When was the Lumen Valley Water Cooperative founded?",
 "reference": "12 April 1958", "tags": ["rag", "answerable", "history"], "difficulty": "easy",
 "metadata": {"answerable": true, "evidence": [{"doc_id": "history.md", "text": "The cooperative was founded on 12 April 1958 by ..."}]}}

The corpus is fictional so that answers cannot come from a model's pretraining data. It is small: retrieval metrics on 20 answerable questions and abstention on 5 unanswerable ones have wide intervals.

docs.title: 8. Limitations
docs.text:
• Lexical defaults. The hash embedder, the lexical verifier and the 0.6 evidence rule measure word overlap. Paraphrased evidence, paraphrased answers and contradictions that reuse the context's words are misjudged. Use a sentence-embedding model and verifier: judge (with a calibrated judge) for real evaluations.
  • Gold evidence quality. Retrieval metrics are only as good as the annotated passages. A chunk containing equally valid evidence that was not annotated counts as irrelevant.
  • Coarse claims. Sentences are not atomic facts; one unsupported clause makes the whole sentence unsupported, and hallucination flags any answer with one unsupported sentence.
  • Heuristic abstention. Abstention detection is phrase matching (METHODOLOGY.md, 2.8). A model that abstains in other words is scored as answering.
  • Sweep statistics. One answer per question, per-setting CIs only, no multiplicity control when choosing a best setting, main effects ignore interactions.
  • Mock generator. It reads the evidence through the oracle. Mock sweeps validate the plumbing and show that retrieval quality propagates to answers, not how any model behaves.
  • Scale. The in-memory store is exact and fine for small corpora; pgvector as configured here does an exact scan without an ANN index.

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records
docs.text:
Each record captures one significant design decision in LLMBench: the context that forced it, what was decided, its positive and negative consequences, and the alternatives that were rejected. Every statement in a record refers to code that can be checked; module paths are relative to src/llmbench/ unless stated otherwise.

ADR Title Status Main code 0001 SQLite run store via SQLAlchemy 2.0 and Alembic Accepted tracking/db.py, tracking/store.py, tracking/migrate.py, tracking/bundle.py 0002 Async runner with a fixed worker pool and per-model resilience controls Accepted runner/executor.py, runner/rate_limit.py, runner/retry.py, runner/circuit.py, runner/budget.py, runner/clock.py 0003 Response cache keyed per trial, including model params and base URL Accepted runner/cache.py 0004 Cluster bootstrap for intervals, paired per-sample tests for comparisons Accepted stats/bootstrap.py, stats/compare.py, stats/paired.py 0005 LLM-as-a-judge with structured output and explicit bias controls Accepted judges/judge.py, judges/metrics.py, judges/factory.py, judges/calibration.py 0006 Typed registries with lazy entry-point discovery for plugins Accepted plugins/registry.py, metrics/base.py, providers/registry.py, tasks/base.py 0007 A deterministic, oracle-driven mock provider Accepted providers/mock.py 0008 Chat Completions for OpenAI-style servers, google-genai for Gemini, SDK retries off Accepted providers/openai_provider.py, providers/gemini_provider.py, providers/_http.py 0009 Static web dashboard with demo (CI JSON) and live (REST API + CORS) modes Accepted frontend/, scripts/build_site.sh, api/app.py

docs.title: How the records relate
docs.text:
• 0001 (storage) underpins 0002 (per-trial checkpointing and resume) and 0003 (the cache lives in the run database).
  • 0002 owns retries, which is why 0008 disables SDK-level retries.
  • 0004 defines the statistics that the CI gate in ../CI_EVAL_GATE.md builds on; 0007 makes that gate testable offline with a known seeded regression.
  • 0005 and 0006 describe extension points (judge rubrics, plugins) listed in ../ARCHITECTURE.md.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Every record uses the same sections:

  1. Title (# ADR NNNN: ...)
  2. Status (Proposed, Accepted, Superseded by NNNN or Deprecated)
  3. Date (ISO 8601)
  4. Context

  6. Consequences, split into positive and negative
  7. Alternatives considered

  2. Write it in the past tense for facts and the present tense for the decision; name the modules involved so a reader can verify each claim.
