docs.title: ADR 0001: SQLite run store via SQLAlchemy 2.0 and Alembic
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Every trial LLMBench executes costs time and, against real providers, money. Results must survive crashes and Ctrl-C, be queryable later for comparison, drift detection and gating, and carry enough provenance (config, manifest, dataset hash) to explain where a number came from. The tool is mostly run on a laptop or in a short-lived CI job, where running a database server is friction. The API service (llmbench serve) and the CLI should share one storage layer.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Persist everything in a relational store accessed through SQLAlchemy 2.0 ORM models (tracking/db.py): runs, trials, metric_values, judge_calls, baselines, cache_entries and artifacts. Flexible payloads (config, manifest, tags, parsed output, metric details, cached responses) use the generic JSON column type.
  • Default URL is sqlite:///.llmbench/llmbench.db (config/settings.py); make_engine creates the parent directory. Any SQLAlchemy URL can be supplied with LLMBENCH_DB_URL or the global --db option, so Postgres is possible without code changes.
  • On SQLite, a connect listener sets PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON, journal_mode=WAL and synchronous=NORMAL.
  • The schema is owned by Alembic migrations packaged inside the wheel (tracking/migrations/, currently 0001_initial_schema). tracking/migrate.py builds the Alembic config programmatically, so no alembic.ini is needed, and RunStore.__init__ upgrades to head on every open. render_as_batch=True keeps SQLite ALTER migrations workable. test_migrations_match_models asserts the ORM models and migrations never drift.
  • RunStore (tracking/store.py) is the only repository. It uses short, synchronous sessions (session.begin() per operation, expire_on_commit=False).
  • add_trial writes and commits one trial at a time; the trial is the checkpoint unit that resume relies on (completed_trial_keys).
  • Writes are issued synchronously from the asyncio event loop (runner workers, API job queue). This is accepted because a run spends almost all of its wall time awaiting provider calls, and a local SQLite commit in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL does not fsync the database on every commit. Moving writes to a thread would add a second concurrency domain for little gain at the concurrency levels the runner targets.
  • Portable run bundles (tracking/bundle.py, format llmbench-run/1) export a run's metadata, manifest, trials and metric values to JSON and import them into another store. CI commits a bundle as the stored baseline instead of sharing a database file (see docs/CI_EVAL_GATE.md).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Zero-setup persistence: the first llmbench run creates a working database.
  • Crash safety at trial granularity; an interrupted run resumes exactly where it stopped.
  • One schema serves CLI, API, reports, comparisons and gates; migrations are versioned and tested, and upgrades happen automatically on open.
  • Bundles make baselines reviewable in a pull request and independent of any database.

Negative:

  • Synchronous commits briefly block the event loop. With a remote database (Postgres over a network) each commit adds a round trip on the loop; with the mock provider and time_scale: 0 the database is the bottleneck. Neither matters for correctness.
  • SQLite allows a single writer. Several processes writing to one file (for example two CI jobs on a shared volume) will contend; use separate files or Postgres.
  • Postgres support is by construction (generic types, no SQLite-only SQL in the store), but the offline test suite only exercises SQLite, and no Postgres driver is a core dependency.
  • Auto-upgrade on open means an older LLMBench cannot be trusted to open a database that a newer version migrated.
  • Bundle export stores the dataset path and base_dir relative to the project root (the working directory at export time) and llmbench import --base-dir (default .) resolves them again, so export and import must both run from the project root. A path outside that root keeps the exporting machine's absolute path. Gating does not need the path; re-evaluating an imported run does.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• JSONL files per run. Simple and diff-friendly, but every comparison would re-implement indexing and joins, and concurrent appends need their own locking. Bundles keep the diff-friendly property where it matters (committed baselines).
  • DuckDB or Parquet as the primary store. Strong for analytics, weaker for many small transactional writes from concurrent workers. Parquet remains an export format.
  • An async driver (aiosqlite, SQLAlchemy asyncio). Removes loop blocking but adds a dependency and async session management across every caller (CLI, reports, stats) for a cost that is small relative to provider latency.
  • Require Postgres. Better multi-writer behaviour, but defeats the offline, keyless, single-command workflow that tests, the quickstart and CI depend on.

docs.title: ADR 0002: Async runner with a fixed worker pool and per-model resilience controls
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: An experiment is a grid of models x prompts x samples x trials; a modest config easily reaches thousands of provider calls. Calls are I/O-bound, subject to provider rate limits, fail transiently, cost money, and may be interrupted by the user. Results must be reproducible and an interrupted run must be resumable without redoing finished work. The executor must be testable without real time passing.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The executor (runner/executor.py) is a single-process asyncio design:

  • Lazy, trial-major grid. PreparedExperiment.iter_items() (runner/prepare.py) is a generator ordered trial -> sample -> model -> prompt, so a partial run covers every configuration evenly. concurrency workers (default 8) run in an asyncio.TaskGroup and pull from one shared iterator that skips keys already persisted. Memory stays flat for large grids.
  • Trial keys. model_id|prompt_id|sample_id|trial_index is unique per run (enforced by uq_trials_run_key) and is the unit of checkpointing and resume.
  • Rate limiting (runner/rate_limit.py). A RateLimiter combines a requests-per-minute and a tokens-per-minute TokenBucket; burst capacity is one second's worth (at least 1). The token estimate is prompt characters / 4 plus max_tokens (512 if unset), clamped to the bucket capacity. One limiter and one breaker are built per provider endpoint, keyed by (provider, base_url, api_key_env) in _build_slots, and shared by every model that uses that endpoint, because providers enforce limits per account and endpoint. Limits come from the first such model's rate_limit or the experiment-level one. (An earlier version built them per model spec; sharing exposed a float-precision livelock in TokenBucket, fixed with a tolerance and a 1 ms minimum wait.)
  • Retries (runner/retry.py). Only TIMEOUT, RATE_LIMITED, SERVER_ERROR and NETWORK are retryable (RETRYABLE_ERRORS in providers/base.py); AUTH, INVALID_REQUEST, CONTENT_FILTERED, REFUSAL and MALFORMED_OUTPUT are not. The delay is full jitter, U(0, min(max_delay_s, base_delay_s * 2**(attempt-1))), floored by a server Retry-After capped at 300 s. Each attempt is bounded by asyncio.wait_for(timeout_s).
  • Circuit breaker (runner/circuit.py). Opens after failure_threshold consecutive failures (default 8), waits reset_timeout_s (default 30), then admits a single half-open probe; success closes it, failure re-opens it. INVALID_REQUEST and CONTENT_FILTERED do not count. After MAX_BREAKER_TRIPS = 3 openings the endpoint is abandoned for the run: every model on it stops retrying and its remaining items are skipped, leaving the run partial.
  • Budget (runner/budget.py). Before a call the worker reserves an estimated cost (estimated input tokens plus the output ceiling, priced from pricing.yaml); reservations make max_usd safe under concurrency. After the call the reservation is settled with the actual cost (0 for failed calls). Exceeding max_usd or max_requests raises BudgetExceededError, which stops all workers gracefully with status budget_exceeded.
  • Checkpointing and resume. Each finished trial (success or classified failure) is written immediately with RunStore.add_trial. Runner.resume rebuilds the config from the manifest, restricts samples to the manifest's sample ids, refuses if the evaluated dataset hash changed or a model is no longer runnable, and executes only missing keys.
  • SIGINT. cli._execute installs loop.add_signal_handler(SIGINT, runner.request_stop). Workers finish their in-flight trial, the run is marked interrupted, metrics are computed on what exists, and the CLI prints llmbench resume <run_id>.
  • Injectable clock (runner/clock.py). Rate limiter, retry sleeps and breaker use a Clock protocol; tests pass FakeClock, whose sleep advances virtual time instantly.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Bounded memory and concurrency for any grid size; trial-major order makes partial results comparable across configurations.
  • Interruption, budget stops and crashes lose at most the in-flight trials. The integration test test_interrupt_and_resume_matches_uninterrupted_run checks that a resumed run's outputs equal an uninterrupted run's on the mock provider.
  • Every attempt is visible: attempts, queue_wait_ms, error_class are recorded per trial.
  • Rate limiting, backoff and breaker logic are tested deterministically and fast.

Negative:

  • Limits are per model spec, not per provider account: two models on the same key each get the full configured rate, so the experiment-level rate_limit should be set to the account limit divided by the number of models sharing it.
  • Estimates are coarse (characters / 4). Unpriced models reserve 0, so max_usd does not protect them; max_requests counts trials, not retry attempts.
  • A stop request is checked between trials only; a trial already in its retry loop continues until it succeeds or exhausts its attempts.
  • resume verifies the dataset hash but re-reads prompt templates and the pricing file from disk without comparing them to the hashes stored in the manifest.
  • Single process: throughput is bounded by one event loop. Horizontal scale needs several runs or the API behind a real queue (see ARCHITECTURE.md).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Thread pool. Simpler with blocking SDKs but heavier per task, harder to cancel, and the SDKs used here are async-native.
  • asyncio.gather over the materialised grid. Trivial code, but memory grows with the grid and concurrency control moves into semaphores sprinkled across the call path.
  • SDK-level retries. Hides attempts from the trial record and cannot share a breaker or a budget; see ADR 0008.
  • A third-party retry library (tenacity). Capable, but Retry-After flooring, the breaker interplay and fake-clock testing were simpler to own in about 40 lines.

docs.title: ADR 0003: Response cache keyed per trial, including model params and base URL
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Re-running an unchanged experiment (to regenerate a report, tweak a metric, or recover from a crash in evaluation) should not pay for the same provider calls twice. A naive prompt-level cache breaks the statistics, though: LLMBench runs each prompt several times (trials) precisely to measure variability, and if trial 2 returned trial 1's cached text every consistency metric, pass@k and cluster-bootstrap interval would be computed over copies of one sample.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
runner/cache.py implements a read-through cache stored in the run database (cache_entries table, ADR 0001). The key is the SHA-256 of a canonical JSON payload (canonical_json: sorted keys, compact separators) containing:

  • provider: the provider name (mock, openai, openai_compat, gemini, or a plugin);
  • model_config: the model spec's full params mapping and its base_url;
  • model: the provider-side model name;
  • params: the normalised GenerationParams (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, seed, stop, json_mode, stream);
  • messages: the rendered system and user messages;
  • trial_index.

Rules:

  • Trial index in the key. Repeated trials stay independent samples. Re-running the same config replays the same trial 0..n-1 outputs, which keeps re-runs identical while still having n distinct draws per sample.
  • Model params and base URL in the key. Added by commit "fix(runner): include model params and base_url in the response-cache key". Before it, only the normalised GenerationParams were hashed, so provider-specific knobs that live in params but not in GenerationParams were invisible to the key. A test changing the mock provider's accuracy hit stale entries and reported the old behaviour. The same flaw would have let two OpenAI-compatible servers serving the same model name under different base_urls share entries. test_cache_key_includes_trial_index_and_params now covers this.
  • Only successful results are cached (ResponseCache.put returns early unless result.ok). Transient failures are retried on the next run instead of being replayed.
  • Cached trials are recorded with cached=True, one attempt and zero queue wait. Their cost_usd is computed from the original call's token counts with the run's pricing table, so per-configuration cost reports stay comparable. They skip budget reservation and are not added to BudgetGuard.spent_usd (no money is spent), so a fully cached re-run reports spent $0.0000 while runs.total_cost_usd still sums the nominal trial costs.
  • Caching is on by default; it can be disabled per experiment (cache: false), per invocation (--no-cache on run, resume, rerun), and cleared with llmbench cache clear. A run's manifest records cache_enabled, which resume honours.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Re-running an identical config is free and instant, and produces identical trial outputs (test_cache_makes_rerun_free).
  • Trials remain statistically independent draws; cached and uncached runs have the same shape.
  • Any parameter a user can set on a model now invalidates its entries.

Negative:

  • The key uses the requested model name, not the version the provider actually served. If a provider re-points an alias, cached entries keep returning the old model's outputs. Drift monitoring and baseline refreshes should use --no-cache.
  • GenerationRequest.metadata is not part of the key. Real providers never see it, but the mock reads its oracle: editing a sample's reference without changing its input can replay an answer computed against the old reference.
  • Hashing the whole params mapping also includes knobs that cannot change the output (for example timeout_s), so changing them causes cache misses.
  • The cache grows without bound until cleared; cache_clear(older_than=...) exists in the store but the CLI exposes only a full clear.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Prompt-level key (no trial index). Maximises hits but collapses repeated trials into one sample, invalidating consistency metrics and confidence intervals.
  • Hash only GenerationParams. The original implementation; it missed provider-specific parameters and base_url, as described above.
  • Cache failures too. Would make reruns faster on flaky providers but would freeze transient errors into results.
  • External cache (Redis, on-disk key-value store). Another moving part; the run database already provides durable storage and is shared by CLI and API.

docs.title: ADR 0004: Cluster bootstrap for intervals, paired per-sample tests for comparisons
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: LLM outputs vary between trials of the same input, and inputs vary in difficulty. Benchmarks are usually small (tens to hundreds of samples) and metrics are often binary. Treating each trial as an independent observation understates uncertainty, because trials of one sample are correlated. Comparisons between two configurations are evaluated on the same samples, so the pairing should be exploited. A CI gate built on these numbers must not fail on noise, and when many metrics are compared at once the family-wise error must be controlled.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Statistics live in src/llmbench/stats/ and are implemented directly on numpy and scipy:

  • Per-configuration intervals use a two-stage cluster bootstrap (cluster_bootstrap_ci in bootstrap.py): stage 1 resamples samples with replacement, stage 2 resamples trials within each chosen sample. The estimate is the mean of per-sample means, so every sample weighs equally regardless of how many trials succeeded. This is used by run summaries (reporting/summary.py, 1000 resamples) and by comparisons (2000 resamples).
  • Paired comparisons (compare_metric in compare.py) align the two runs on common sample ids and reduce each side to per-sample means. The default test (choose_test) is:
  • McNemar (mcnemar_test) when the metric is binary and both sides have exactly one trial per sample (exact binomial below 25 discordant pairs, continuity-corrected chi-square above);
  • otherwise a sign-flip permutation test on the per-sample differences (paired_permutation_test): exact enumeration up to 16 non-zero differences, else 10,000 Monte Carlo flips with the +1 correction so p is never 0. Wilcoxon and a paired bootstrap test are available by name.
  • Delta interval: a paired bootstrap over per-sample differences (paired_bootstrap).
  • Effect sizes: Cliff's delta for binary metrics, Cohen's d_z otherwise (effect.py); the minimum detectable effect (power.py, normal approximation, power 0.8) is reported, with a warning below 30 paired samples.
  • Multiple comparisons: p-values within one configuration pair are adjusted across metrics with Holm by default (correction.py); Benjamini-Hochberg and none are selectable.
  • Verdict (_verdict): improved or regressed only when the adjusted p < alpha AND the delta CI excludes 0; otherwise no significant change; fewer than 2 aligned samples gives insufficient data. The gate (tracking/gates.py) adds a practical-size threshold on top.
  • BCa (bca_ci, Efron 1987, jackknife acceleration, percentile fallback when degenerate) and a percentile bootstrap are part of the public llmbench.stats API. The run pipeline does not call BCa; the RAG sweep uses the percentile interval over per-question values.
  • All resampling uses numpy.random.default_rng with fixed seeds, so a comparison of the same two stored runs is reproducible.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Intervals widen correctly when trials are correlated; test_stats.py checks the cluster interval against a naive flat bootstrap on highly clustered data, and BCa coverage on a known distribution.
  • Reducing to per-sample means makes the paired tests valid for any number of trials and for continuous and binary metrics alike.
  • Requiring both significance and a CI that excludes zero, plus Holm, keeps false regressions rare; a property test asserts identical configurations never produce a regressed verdict.
  • Every step is short, readable code that can be audited against textbook definitions.

Negative:

  • Per-sample means discard within-sample information that a mixed-effects model would use, so tests are conservative when trials are many and samples few.
  • The permutation test assumes symmetric differences under H0; the bootstrap and normal-theory MDE are approximate for very small n (hence the warning).
  • McNemar on per-sample means thresholds at 0.5, which is only meaningful for single-trial binary metrics, the only case in which it is selected.
  • Maintaining statistical code in-house means correctness rests on our own tests rather than on a widely used library's.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Flat (i.i.d.) bootstrap over trials. Simpler; understates uncertainty with repeated trials.
  • Welch t-test on trial values. Ignores pairing and clustering; poor for binary metrics.
  • scipy.stats.bootstrap / permutation_test. Capable, but neither implements a two-stage cluster bootstrap, and wrapping them obscures exactly which unit is resampled.
  • Mixed-effects or Bayesian hierarchical models. More statistically efficient, but add heavy dependencies and assumptions that are harder to explain in a CI failure message.
  • BCa as the default interval. Better small-sample coverage for skewed statistics, but its jackknife does not extend cleanly to the two-stage cluster case; it stays available for single-level data.

docs.title: ADR 0005: LLM-as-a-judge with structured output and explicit bias controls
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Lexical metrics miss correct paraphrases, so LLMBench offers an LLM judge (llm_judge_correctness). LLM judges have documented failure modes: inconsistent scales, free text that does not parse, preference for the first-presented answer (position bias), for longer answers (length bias) and for their own outputs (self-preference), sampling noise, and unknown agreement with humans. A judge score that silently carries these biases would undermine the statistics built on it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Implemented in src/llmbench/judges/:

  • Rubrics with anchors (rubric.py, e.g. rubrics/correctness.yaml): named, weighted criteria, an integer scale (default 1-5), a pass_threshold, and per-score anchor descriptions with optional examples. The rubric is validated (threshold and anchors inside the scale). The system prompt tells the judge to ignore length and style unless the rubric says otherwise and to treat candidate text as data, not instructions.
  • Structured output with validation and repair (judge.py): every call requests JSON (json_mode), the reply is parsed with extract_json and validated against a JSON Schema (Draft202012Validator; integer score within the scale, or winner in A/B/tie). On failure the judge is re-prompted with the validation error, up to max_repairs times (default 2); a still-invalid reply yields no score and an error, never a guessed score.
  • Temperature 0 by default (JudgeSpec.params and LLMJudge default to {"temperature": 0.0}).
  • Position swap for pairwise judging (LLMJudge.pairwise, swap_order=True by default): both orders are judged and mapped back to the inputs; if they disagree the result is a tie with position_consistent=False.
  • Length bias reporting: length_bias computes the Spearman correlation between answer length and normalised score; the run summary recomputes it from the persisted per-trial details.length and shows it in the report.
  • Self-preference warning: build_judge (factory.py) logs judge_is_candidate when the judge's provider and model equal a candidate's; the summary also flags candidate_overlap when the judge model name appears among the run's models.
  • Self-consistency: samples > 1 collects independent judgments; the score is their mean and self_consistency is the modal share. Repeat calls use distinct trial_index values.
  • Calibration against humans (calibration.py, llmbench judge calibrate): runs the judge on a labelled JSONL set and reports accuracy, Cohen's kappa (pass/fail), quadratic-weighted kappa and Spearman on scores when human scores exist, the confusion matrix and mean self-consistency. --attach <run> stores the report as a run artifact shown in the report.
  • Audit trail: every judge call, including repairs and provider errors, is written to the judge_calls table with prompt, raw output, parsed result, tokens, cost, latency and error (run_id is null for calibration calls).
  • Failed candidate trials score 0 without calling the judge; a judge failure leaves the value null, so it is excluded rather than counted as wrong.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Judge scores are reproducible to the extent the provider honours temperature 0, parse failures are explicit, and every number can be traced to the exact prompt and reply.
  • Biases are measured and surfaced rather than assumed away; calibration gives a number (kappa) to decide whether a judge is fit for gating.
  • The mock provider simulates judging (token-overlap scores, malformed JSON, position_bias), so all of this is tested offline.

Negative:

  • Judge calls bypass the runner: no rate limiter, retry policy, circuit breaker, cache or budget applies, and judge cost is not counted against max_usd. A provider error fails that judgment immediately.
  • Position swap applies only to pairwise judging, which is available through the Python API; no built-in metric or CLI command currently uses it. Pointwise scoring has no order to swap.
  • Length bias is reported, not corrected. Per-item self-consistency is returned by the judge but not persisted in metric details, so for normal runs it is only visible in calibration reports.
  • The self-preference check compares names only; a fine-tune or alias of the same base model is not detected.
  • With samples > 1 and repairs, one judged trial can cost several calls.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Free-text judge output parsed with regex. Fragile; silently misreads scores.
  • Logprob-weighted scores. Not uniformly available across the supported providers.
  • Pairwise-only judging. Strong for A/B but needs a partner answer for every item and does not give an absolute score for gating.
  • Discard length-biased judges automatically. No principled threshold; reporting the correlation leaves the decision to the user with calibration data at hand.

docs.title: ADR 0006: Typed registries with lazy entry-point discovery for plugins
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Users need to add their own providers (an internal gateway, a self-hosted model), metrics (domain-specific checks) and task types (custom pass criteria) without forking LLMBench. Built-ins and plugins should be referenced the same way from experiment YAML (provider:, metrics:, task:), listed by the CLI, and fail with a clear message when a name is unknown. Importing LLMBench should stay cheap and not import every installed plugin eagerly.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• One generic class, Registry[T] (plugins/registry.py), holds a name -> object mapping for one plugin kind and an entry-point group. Built-ins register at import time. On a lookup miss (get) or when listing (names), the registry loads its entry-point group once (importlib.metadata.entry_points). Built-in names win over entry points with the same name; explicit register refuses to overwrite an existing different object unless replace=True; unknown names raise RegistryError listing what is registered.
  • Three registries and groups, declared (empty) in pyproject.toml:
  • PROVIDERS / llmbench.providers (providers/registry.py): a factory (ModelSpec, Settings) -> Provider. Built-ins mock, openai, openai_compat and gemini register with PROVIDERS.decorator(...); the SDK-backed factories import their adapter module lazily inside the factory. A provider implements the Provider protocol (generate, embed, aclose, name) and raises ProviderError with an ErrorClass so retries and the breaker work.
  • METRICS / llmbench.metrics (metrics/base.py): a callable returning a Metric (normally the class). @register_metric registers a Metric subclass; @trial_metric(name, higher_is_better=..., kind=...) turns fn(trial, sample) into a registered TrialMetric. GroupMetric covers per-sample metrics over repeated trials. Each metric declares higher_is_better and kind (binary or continuous), which the comparison and gate use to pick a test and a direction.
  • TASKS / llmbench.tasks (tasks/base.py): a Task instance providing parse, is_pass, oracle, default_metrics and json_output.
  • llmbench providers, llmbench metrics and llmbench tasks list everything registered, including plugins.

A third-party package exposes plugins in its own pyproject.toml:

[project.entry-points."llmbench.providers"]
my_gateway = "my_pkg.llmbench_plugin:gateway_factory"

[project.entry-points."llmbench.metrics"]
mentions_source = "my_pkg.llmbench_plugin:MentionsSource"

[project.entry-points."llmbench.tasks"]
ticket_routing = "my_pkg.llmbench_plugin:TICKET_ROUTING_TASK"

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • One mechanism, three plugin kinds; YAML names resolve identically for built-ins and plugins.
  • Entry points load lazily, so a plain import llmbench does not import installed plugins.
  • Typed protocols and base classes give plugin authors a small, documented surface; metrics inherit failure handling (error_value) and per-sample result shapes from the base classes.

Negative:

  • Entry points are loaded as-is: a provider entry must be a factory function, a metric entry a Metric class (or factory), and a task entry an instance, not a class. Nothing validates the loaded object's type at load time; a mistake surfaces on first use.
  • A plugin that fails to import raises on the first registry miss or listing. The registry marks its group as loaded before iterating, so entry points after the broken one are not loaded for the rest of the process.
  • Plugins run in-process with full privileges; installing one is equivalent to running its code.
  • check_availability only knows the built-in providers' requirements (API keys, base_url); a plugin provider is treated as available, and missing credentials appear at call time.
  • Plugin metrics not registered under the name used in a stored run fall back to higher-is-better, continuous defaults in metric_direction.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Import-path strings in YAML (metric: my_pkg.module:Class). No packaging step, but ties configs to module layout and executes arbitrary imports named in data files.
  • pluggy hooks. Mature, but hook specifications add ceremony for what are plain lookups.
  • A single registry for all kinds. Fewer objects, but loses typing and allows name clashes across kinds.
  • Eager entry-point loading at import. Simpler control flow, slower startup, and any broken plugin would break every command.

docs.title: ADR 0007: A deterministic, oracle-driven mock provider
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: LLMBench must be testable and demonstrable without API keys or network access: the unit and integration tests, the quickstart, the llmbench init scaffold and the repository's own CI gate all need a provider. A trivial echo stub would not exercise what LLMBench is for: variability across trials, a controllable quality level, failures that trigger retries and the circuit breaker, judge parsing, RAG citations and safety probes. Resume must also be checkable, which requires the same trial to produce the same output on re-execution.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
providers/mock.py implements MockProvider, registered as the mock provider:

  • Oracle metadata. The runner attaches metadata["oracle"] (from Task.oracle: sample id, reference, difficulty, task name, sample metadata) to each request. Real adapters never send metadata; the mock uses it to decide whether to answer correctly and to build plausible wrong answers (another label, a perturbed number, a broken JSON field, a filler word).
  • Decisions are a pure function of inputs. Every random draw comes from random.Random seeded with SHA-256 of a tuple built from mock_seed, the model name, the rendered prompt text, the trial index and, for failures and latency, a per-key attempt count.
  • Temperature 0 means identical trials. When the effective temperature is 0 the trial index is dropped from the key, mimicking greedy decoding.
  • Quality model. P(correct) is a logistic function of accuracy, the sample's difficulty (easy +1, hard -1 on the logit) and a per-sample offset drawn with difficulty_seed and scaled by sample_spread.
  • Two seeds. difficulty_seed fixes which samples are hard for a model; mock_seed changes only the sampling noise. Changing mock_seed simulates a re-run of the same system; changing accuracy simulates a real quality change. The gate examples (examples/gate/noise.yaml vs regression.yaml) rely on exactly this split.
  • Failure injection. failure_rate raises ProviderError with a class drawn from error_mix (TIMEOUT / RATE_LIMITED / SERVER_ERROR); simulated 429s carry retry_after_s. Also refusal_rate, malformed_rate, log-normal latency_ms / latency_sigma (slept only as time_scale x latency, default 0), and TTFT when stream is set.
  • Behaviours. Judge mode (metadata["mock_judge"]): pointwise scores from token-F1 against the reference plus noise, pairwise winners with optional position_bias, malformed JSON for repair tests. RAG: cites the numbered context blocks containing gold evidence, abstains when evidence is absent or the question is unanswerable. Safety: obeys an injected instruction (emits the canary) with probability injection_susceptibility.
  • Results carry provider_metadata={"simulated": True}; embeddings come from the deterministic HashEmbedder.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • CI and every test run keyless and offline (pytest deselects live tests by default).
  • Outputs are reproducible across machines and processes; an interrupted and resumed run produces the same trial outputs as an uninterrupted one, which the integration tests assert.
  • Statistical machinery is validated against known ground truth: a seeded regression must be detected, a seed-only change must not.

Negative and risks:

  • Mock numbers can be mistaken for measurements of real models. Mitigations: the HTML report shows a "Mock provider" banner and the Markdown run summary a matching note whenever any configuration uses mock; example configs and CLAUDE.md require mock numbers in docs to be labelled illustrative. The gate Markdown (gate.md) does not carry the banner, so CI summaries from mock runs should say so in the workflow step name.
  • The attempt counter is per provider instance and per key. At temperature 0 all trials of a prompt share one key, so with concurrency > 1 the latency and failure draws a trial receives depend on execution order; the answer text does not.
  • Difficulty is seeded per (sample, model name), so two differently named mock models do not share a difficulty profile.
  • The oracle is excluded from the cache key (ADR 0003); editing a reference without changing the input can replay a stale mock answer.
  • Realism is limited: the mock encodes a simple quality model and cannot stand in for contract tests, which exist separately as @pytest.mark.live tests against real APIs.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Recorded fixtures (VCR-style cassettes). Realistic text, but fixed to recorded prompts, break whenever a prompt changes, cannot produce new trials, and need keys to re-record.
  • A small local model. Real generation, but slow, heavy in CI, and not deterministic across hardware without care.
  • Seeding Python's global RNG. Order-dependent under concurrency; hashing the inputs makes each decision independent of scheduling.
  • No oracle (random answers). Every metric would sit near chance and regression detection could not be tested against a known effect.

docs.title: ADR 0008: Chat Completions for OpenAI-style servers, google-genai for Gemini, SDK retries off
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-21

docs.title: Context
docs.text: LLMBench needs adapters for OpenAI, for OpenAI-compatible servers (Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio) and for Gemini. Each adapter must report tokens, latency, time to first token (TTFT), finish reason, refusals and content filtering, and must map failures onto LLMBench's ErrorClass taxonomy. The runner (ADR 0002) owns retries, backoff, the circuit breaker and the budget, so hidden retries inside an SDK would distort attempt counts, latency and cost accounting.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• OpenAI and compatible servers use Chat Completions through the official openai SDK (providers/openai_provider.py, class OpenAIProvider). The same class serves openai and openai_compat, which differ by base_url and by max_tokens_param: max_completion_tokens for OpenAI, max_tokens for compatible servers (providers/registry.py). json_mode maps to response_format={"type": "json_object"}. A non-empty message.refusal maps to REFUSAL; finish_reason == "content_filter" to CONTENT_FILTERED.
  • Streaming for TTFT. With stream: true the adapter streams with stream_options={"include_usage": True} so token usage still arrives in the final chunk, and records TTFT at the first content delta.
  • Gemini uses google-genai (providers/gemini_provider.py): aio.models.generate_content or generate_content_stream, system messages folded into system_instruction, response_mime_type="application/json" for json_mode, prompt block reasons and safety-type finish reasons mapped to CONTENT_FILTERED.
  • SDK retries disabled. AsyncOpenAI(max_retries=0). The Gemini adapter does not set HttpOptions.retry_options; in google-genai 3.x an unset value means a single attempt on the httpx transport. The runner wraps every attempt in asyncio.wait_for(timeout_s) in addition to the SDK timeout.
  • Error mapping. map_openai_error / map_gemini_error translate SDK exceptions; HTTP statuses go through classify_http_status (401/403 AUTH, 429 RATE_LIMITED, 408/504 TIMEOUT, other 5xx SERVER_ERROR, other 4xx INVALID_REQUEST). For OpenAI 429s, parse_retry_after reads retry-after-ms or retry-after (seconds or HTTP date).
  • Transport. The installed SDKs (openai 3.x, google-genai 3.x in .venv) use httpx2, a fork of httpx under a separate import name whose exception classes are not httpx subclasses. Adapters therefore accept a generic http_client (typed Any) that is passed to the SDK unchanged, and tests inject an httpx2.AsyncClient with a MockTransport. providers/_http.py::classify_transport_error checks both httpx and httpx2 TimeoutException and TransportError.
  • SDK imports stay inside these two modules (ruff TID251, see ARCHITECTURE.md) and are performed lazily, so the core installs and runs without either extra.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive:

  • Chat Completions is the API that OpenAI-compatible servers implement, so one adapter covers OpenAI and local or self-hosted models with the same request shape and usage accounting.
  • Every attempt is a runner attempt: attempts, queue_wait_ms, latency and cost are accurate, and Retry-After, breaker and budget logic see every failure.
  • Accepting any client object keeps the adapters working whichever HTTP library the SDK uses.

Negative:

  • Responses-API-only features (built-in tools, server-side conversation state, reasoning summaries) are not reachable through this adapter.
  • Gemini relies on an SDK default for "no retries". If aiohttp is installed and no http_client is passed, google-genai switches to its aiohttp transport, which performs an implicit retry on connection errors, and aiohttp exceptions are not classified by _http.py (they map to SERVER_ERROR). Setting retry options explicitly would remove the dependence on defaults.
  • The Gemini adapter does not extract Retry-After from 429 responses, so its backoff is purely exponential.
  • pyproject.toml floors (openai>=1.40, google-genai>=1.0) predate the httpx2 transport; the offline adapter tests import httpx2 and assume SDK versions that use it.
  • Parameter dialects drift: some compatible servers reject seed or response_format, which surfaces as INVALID_REQUEST (not retried).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• OpenAI Responses API. The newer OpenAI interface with richer features, but most OpenAI-compatible servers do not implement it, so it would require a second adapter for the same model families and different usage fields. Can be added later as a separate provider.
  • Raw HTTP with httpx for every provider. Full control and one transport, but duplicates auth, streaming parsing and schema handling that the SDKs maintain.
  • Keep SDK retries on. Fewer moving parts, but attempts become invisible, retries stack with the runner's (multiplying load during an outage), and the breaker sees fewer failures.
  • A multi-provider abstraction library. Broad coverage, but an extra layer between LLMBench and the provider that obscures error classes, usage fields and retry behaviour.

docs.title: ADR 0009: Static web dashboard with demo and live modes
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-24

docs.title: Context
docs.text: The HTML report is per run and generated offline. People evaluating LLMBench (and teams using it) also want to browse results interactively, compare runs and launch benchmarks without a terminal. The project must stay free to host and free to run.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• A single-page dashboard in frontend/ built with React and TypeScript (strict), bundled by Vite. Charts are hand-written SVG components (CI bars, Pareto scatter, histogram, forest plot) using CSS colour tokens with light and dark themes, so there is no chart dependency.
  • Demo mode reads static JSON produced in CI by scripts/build_site.sh (llmbench report --format json, compare --format json, check --json, rag sweep --json, judge calibration). It needs no backend and is always on.
  • Live mode talks to any LLMBench REST API. The browser sends X-API-Key; the API allows the dashboard origin through LLMBENCH_CORS_ORIGINS (off by default). The key is stored only in the browser's local storage.
  • The build is served from the same GitHub Pages site as the docs, at /app/, with a relative base path so any static host works.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
Positive: zero hosting cost, no server needed for the demo, the same view components render demo and live data because both use the API's response models, and CI type-checks and builds the dashboard on every push.

Negative: the TypeScript types mirror the pydantic models by hand and must be kept in sync. Live mode depends on the API being reachable from the browser (CORS, free-tier wake-up time). Storing an API key in local storage is acceptable for a personal deployment but not for a shared, multi-user one, which would need real authentication.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Server-rendered pages in FastAPI: would couple the UI to a running server and cost money to keep online.
  • Streamlit / Gradio: fast to build but needs a Python server for every view and gives less control over the visual design.
  • A charting library (Recharts, Plotly): larger bundle and less control over accessible, theme-aware styling for a handful of chart types.

Everything in this folder was generated on 2026-11-21 by running LLMBench in this repository with LLMBench's deterministic mock provider. No API keys were available in the environment that produced it, so no real model was called. The numbers show what the reports look like and exercise every statistic end to end; they are not measurements of any real model.

File Command that produced it quickstart.html llmbench run examples/quickstart.yaml then llmbench report <run> -o docs/example-report/quickstart.html quickstart.md llmbench report <run> --format md comparison.md llmbench compare <run> <run> --pair mock-fast/v1=mock-fast/v2 --pair mock-fast/v2=mock-strong/v2 --metric ... --format md judge_calibration.json, .txt llmbench judge calibrate datasets/judge_calibration.jsonl --config examples/quickstart.yaml --attach <run> safety.md llmbench run examples/safety.yaml then llmbench report latest --format md rag_sweep.md llmbench rag sweep examples/rag_sweep.yaml --output docs/example-report/rag_sweep.md --top 8 report-screenshot.png top of quickstart.html, light theme

How to read the mock numbers: the mock's accuracy knob is a target on the logit scale with per-sample difficulty, so observed pass rates differ from the nominal value (see METHODOLOGY.md). The mock judge scores answers by token overlap with the reference, which is why its calibration against the human labels is only moderate (Cohen's kappa 0.333 on 40 labelled examples in this run): it penalises correct but verbose answers. That is exactly the kind of weakness calibration is meant to expose.

To produce a real report, export OPENAI_API_KEY and/or GEMINI_API_KEY, set real model names in examples/experiment.yaml, and run llmbench run examples/experiment.yaml.
